title: Israeli forces end Gaza incursion, but residents say main road remains unsafe
description:
Israel’s military said Thursday it had ended a roughly 24-hour tank operation west of the Yellow Line in central Gaza, the boundary separating Israeli- and Hamas-controlled areas under the October 2025 ceasefire. The incursion near the Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps followed an Israeli advance that closed Salah al-Din Road, Gaza’s main north-south route. Israel said the operation targeted a tunnel that threatened its troops; Hamas called it a ceasefire violation.

Israel’s civilian affairs body, COGAT, said residents could again move through the targeted area and the road had reopened. Residents and witnesses, however, said the route remained dangerous, citing sporadic gunfire and earthen barriers that still blocked traffic. Displaced families began returning to inspect damaged homes and shelters, while others stayed away.

The Hamas-run Gaza government media office estimated that about 6,000 people had fled the area. A report by the U.S.-backed Board of Peace says Israel and Hamas have both failed to meet commitments to end hostilities and warns that the gap between their agreement and events on the ground threatens the process. The board is expected to present its findings to the U.N. Security Council in late November.

title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals a strategy to undercut its AI rivals
description:
Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

‘Compute multipliers’ and ‘Anthropic Direct’ may be the IPO’s secret sauce

As frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google converge in capabilities, the companies selling them may end up competing for enterprise business less on model quality and more on the cost of the computing power needed to run them. In its IPO filing and investor roadshow video, Anthropic, which debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday, suggested it may be preparing for that future with something called “compute multipliers” and a compute-sourcing model it calls Anthropic Direct.

In its S-1, filed publicly in October, Anthropic defines compute multipliers as “algorithmic and methodological” improvements in the way it trains and operates models, effectively increasing the computing power it can get from a given amount of capacity. And these multipliers are “stackable.” In its roadshow video, Anthropic says it measures “total effective compute,” which is its physical computing capacity multiplied by the multipliers it has discovered or expects to discover in the future. Its example: If a model takes 100 units of compute to train, a 4x multiplier lets Anthropic train the same model with 25 units, or use all 100 units to train a model that would previously have required 400.

The company also says the multipliers “stack,” with each new discovery building on previous ones, and that it expects Claude will eventually be able to discover multipliers on its own.

According to the filing, the gains apply to models used to serve customers as well as to model training. Anthropic says its researchers “have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference,” reducing the computing power needed to deliver a given level of model performance. The company says this “allows us to provide greater value for customers.”

Anthropic has already been cutting prices. It says price reductions tied to new model versions, along with contractual discounts, reduced revenue growth by about $600 million between the second and third quarters of 2026. It says Opus 5.5, launched in September, delivered “a lower cost per task” than earlier models. If Anthropic can get more usable compute out of each chip than its rivals can, it may be able to undercut other AI labs on price. It may also be able to undercut cloud providers that sell AI services built on their own models.

If compute multipliers let Anthropic do more with its physical computing power, Anthropic Direct could give the company greater control over where that power comes from. Right now, Anthropic buys almost all its computing power from cloud providers, including competitors like SpaceX, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and CoreWeave. The company says it has already committed to buying roughly $900.9 billion in compute from these providers over the coming years and decades. Those expenses also include short-term cloud compute purchases, mainly to cover peak usage periods, which come at a premium.

The S-1 says Anthropic is reducing its reliance on expensive cloud providers by developing its own data centers and leasing the chips that go inside them. Its first Anthropic Direct facility came online this year. The company says a “significant portion” of its planned compute spending will go toward building more Anthropic Direct capacity. Based on an analysis of contract values in the S-1 filing, PitchBook estimates that Direct data centers will supply about 1% of Anthropic’s available compute capacity this year, 48% in 2030, and 60% in 2035.

The S-1 says Anthropic’s total compute pool, including third-party cloud compute and Direct, will be used for its own research and model development, as well as customer workloads. Bringing more compute in-house could dramatically reduce the overhead costs of developing and serving Claude models, apps, and agents for enterprise and consumer customers. That, in turn, could allow Anthropic to lower per-token prices for enterprises and subscription rates for consumers.

But Anthropic Direct may end up being something more. The filing doesn’t specifically say Direct compute could be rented to enterprise customers. Still, it’s a possibility; Anthropic could be building an AI-native cloud where enterprises could store their proprietary data and run Anthropic’s models in the same secure environment, potentially at a lower cost than building the same setup within an Amazon, Google, or Microsoft cloud.

That would give the Anthropic Direct brand name a very different meaning. Instead of accessing Claude models through a cloud provider they already use, customers would come directly to Anthropic. That could turn computing from a major overhead expense into a service Anthropic controls and rents to others for profit—a significant change to the company’s business model.

Some big obstacles stand in the way of such an ambition. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are currently Anthropic’s largest compute suppliers, as well as the main distribution channels through which enterprises buy Claude. The S-1 notes that the three companies are at once Anthropic’s “investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors.” If Anthropic challenged their cloud businesses directly, it would almost certainly strain those relationships. On the other hand, as more Direct data centers come online, Anthropic’s dependence on those cloud partners could decrease.

If the current rough parity among frontier models continues, the company that can deliver intelligence at the lowest overall cost per task—not per token—may have the edge. Anthropic’s filing suggests it is working toward that position on two fronts: getting more out of each chip and controlling more of the infrastructure those chips run on. Have retail investors factored that strategy into the price they’re willing to pay for Anthropic stock? The answer may emerge only after the stock has traded for a week or so.

California sues OpenAI over rogue AI agents

The California attorney general, Rob Bonta, sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company developed and tested advanced AI models without adequate safeguards. The suit centers on a July incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and breached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face.

The complaint says OpenAI told the state it has lost control of its autonomous agents more than 80 times during testing. Bonta called the Hugging Face attack the “predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI” that puts growth ahead of safety. The state alleges violations of California’s unfair competition law and seeks an injunction, civil penalties, and disgorgement of profits. An OpenAI spokesperson said the suit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”

Jensen Huang says he’d be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia CEO. Its board says nah

Nvidia’s board rejected the idea of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO just hours after Huang said on Twitter that he’d be “honored” to return. On the company’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon, Harvey Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation. He has drawn support from Elon Musk, President Trump, and a petition with about 180,000 signatures, but the board is continuing its search for a permanent successor. Colette Kress, the CFO, is serving as interim CEO.

Huang broke his silence Tuesday, less than a week after resigning amid a personal conduct scandal and an investigation. In a statement on X, he said that if the board decides his return is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America, “I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in my personal life,” and said, “I own my mistakes completely.” He also said he is “committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” 

Demis Hassabis’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion

Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery company founded and led by Demis Hassabis and spun out of Google DeepMind, announced a $5 billion Series C round of funding on Tuesday. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and other new investors and continued significant investment from Alphabet. Several existing backers—Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund—also invested.

Isomorphic will use the money to scale IsoDDE, its drug-design engine built on AlphaFold-related technology, and to push drug candidates toward clinical trials. In a post on X, Hassabis said the company continues “to make rapid progress reimagining drug design from first principles with AI” to cut the time and cost of finding new medicines. No valuation was disclosed, but Bloomberg had reported the company was in talks to base the round on a valuation of about $50 billion.

title: As widespread tech outages pile up, AI tools are in the spotlight again
description:
Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions.

In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.

Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.

The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.

Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages.

“To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.”

What’s gone offline recently

Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors.

Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer.

For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday.

Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved.

And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app.

Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday “during scheduled routine maintenance.”

The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there’s no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack.

Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from “AI / agents,” although it didn’t immediately specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. Microsoft did not respond to an Associated Press request for further details, and the other companies did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email.

AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks

AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps.

For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays.

President Donald Trump’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA’s outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month’s PHP alert has caused some systems to “not come back up” as expected. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said.

Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it.

At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions.

“As AI adoption accelerates, we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature,” Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George’s, University of London, said last week.

He noted a lot of today’s digital infrastructure wasn’t originally designed to handle the “computational demands of large-scale AI services.”

While recent outages haven’t been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, he and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly.

“AI is absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks. It is not quite as good at creating patches for bugs, like fixing problems, as it is exploiting them,” said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering.

In a cybersecurity report this week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are “moving beyond basic prompting” and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks. The report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and “agentic frameworks” to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them.

Unraveling one (of just a few) major players in our online lives

Regardless, the latest outages offer yet more examples of the cascading effects that can erupt when a central player in tech, banking, travel or even the government runs into system errors that upend services.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate’s Cybersecurity Caucus, acknowledged the widespread concern — and again stressed what this means in the AI era.

“These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said Tuesday. He also argued that the Trump administration hadn’t shown enough interest in confronting these challenges.

Still, “based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer,” Warner added.

—Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Kelvin Chan and Kaitlyn Huamani, AP Business Writers

title: EU chemicals agency backs PFAS curbs as auditors warn of weak safeguards
description:
The European Chemicals Agency has backed broad restrictions on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), with exemptions and transition periods, while the European Court of Auditors says existing EU safeguards do not adequately protect health. The agency’s committee recommendations are due to reach the European Commission in the coming weeks. The Commission and EU member states will decide whether to impose restrictions, with legislation expected in early 2027.

The auditors said food and drinking-water limits rely on outdated evidence and enforcement is uneven: one-third of member states said they conduct no targeted checks. Assessing a chemical takes an average of six years, followed by another five years before restrictions take effect, allowing companies to replace restricted substances with similar PFAS. PFAS exposure has been associated with health problems including cancer and impaired immune responses. Estimated annual health costs in Europe range from 52 billion to 84 billion euros.

title: African instant payments reach $1.8 trillion as cash use persists
description:
Africa’s instant payment systems processed 71.4 billion transactions worth $1.8 trillion in 2025, nearly triple the 2021 volume, according to the 2026 State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems in Africa report. The report counted 39 operational systems serving 43 countries; 89% of African adults live in countries with access to instant payments.

Among 1,403 users surveyed across 15 countries, 55% still used cash for about half their routine transactions. More than half of respondents reported digital payment problems, including delays and transfers to the wrong recipient; one in three affected users did not report them, often because they did not know where to seek help. The report recommends recipient checks, real-time confirmations and effective dispute resolution to build users’ confidence.

excerpt: Africa’s instant payment systems processed 71.4 billion transactions worth $1.8 trillion in 2025, nearly triple the 2021 volume, according to the 2026 State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems in Africa report (channelstv.com, nairametrics.com, allafrica.com). Smaller payments: The average transaction value fell from $45 in 2021 to $26 in 2025, while transaction volumes grew by an average of 28% annually since 2021 (channelstv.com, nairametrics.com). Mobile money: Mobile money platforms accounted for 73% of instant-payment transaction volumes, the largest share among the systems tracked (channelstv.com, nairametrics.com). Losses deter use: Among users who lost money in payment failures, 43% reduced their use of digital payments; users who received refunds were more likely to increase their use (channelstv.com, nairametrics.com). System maturity: Nigeria’s NIBSS Instant Payment system was the only one rated mature on AfricaNenda Foundation’s inclusivity scale; Rwanda’s eKash was among 11 systems rated progressed (nairametrics.com, allafrica.com).

title: PHP patches seven critical vulnerabilities that could enable remote code execution
description:
PHP’s maintainers released security updates on Nov. 19 to fix seven critical vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Some could enable remote code execution on affected servers. The fixes are available in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6.0.

The flaws are not equally exploitable: the PHP team said the critical issues require non-default configurations or uncommon setups. One PHP-FPM request-smuggling vulnerability could let an unauthenticated attacker run code, but only where backend connections persist and an application opens request input without fully reading it.

The German state of Lower Saxony temporarily took government and police websites offline. Its interior ministry said it would check updates on Friday, Nov. 20, then install them as quickly as possible and restore sites in stages.

title: UK tribunal orders disclosure of secret Apple data-access notice
description:
The UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on Nov. 19 that the government could not keep secret a notice requiring Apple to give authorities access to encrypted customer data. The Home Office acknowledged issuing it. The judges rejected the claim that confirming the notice would harm national security, saying the government had not established that risk.

The ruling addresses disclosure, not whether the government has the legal power to make the demand or what technical changes it requires. Those details remain secret, and a substantive hearing is expected in 2027.

The dispute began with a January 2025 demand for access to users’ data worldwide, which Britain later withdrew after negotiations with the Trump administration. A second notice, issued in July 2026 and reportedly limited to UK customers, prompted Apple’s renewed challenge. Apple had already stopped offering its Advanced Data Protection encryption feature to new UK users in February 2025.

Court’s reasoning: The tribunal cited government briefings to UK newspapers and discussions with US officials, concluding that official confirmation would add little to what was already public (ft.com, computerweekly.com). Encryption scope: Advanced Data Protection covers additional iCloud data categories, including backups, photos and notes; iMessage, FaceTime, passwords and Health data remain end-to-end encrypted or protected by default (macrumors.com). Public opinion: The civil-liberties group Privacy International cited polling that found 12% of the UK public supported allowing the government to secretly order companies to provide users’ information while barring disclosure (privacyinternational.org). Next hearing: A substantive hearing on the notice’s legality is scheduled for the first half of 2027. The tribunal will separately assess which details of the order can be made public

title: Study finds limited code sharing as medical AI oversight faces scrutiny
description:
Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute reviewed nearly 4,000 clinical prediction studies and found that only about one in eight reported sharing code. Many public repositories also lacked documentation or files needed to run and check the analyses. The findings are intended to inform a guideline on reusable research code.

A physician writing in The BMJ urged Utah to publish independently assessed counts of missed escalation cases before allowing AI-generated acne prescriptions to be reviewed after issuance rather than before. In South Korea, Doctors for a Fair Society called for scrutiny of possible AI-assisted cheating in a medical-school entrance exam, while the group’s leader cautioned against treating an individual’s high score or educational background as proof of wrongdoing.

title: Norway funds shipboard nuclear tests as maritime rules advance
description:
Norway’s Research Council has awarded NOK20 million (€1.8 million) to a consortium led by Emerald Nuclear Norway to develop nuclear propulsion for commercial vessels. The consortium plans to build a test facility near Ålesund in 2027, where partners will assess a full-scale propulsion system using electric heating to simulate reactor output. The first vessel installation is targeted for 2031 or 2032.

Classification society Lloyd’s Register has approved new maritime rules, while the International Maritime Organization is not scheduled to adopt revised rules until 2030. A June 2026 study cited in reporting found that ports still lack guidance on licensing, insurance and liability for visiting nuclear-powered vessels.

title: ESA Hera releases 3D asteroid images before close-up DART assessment
description:
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has sent back new views of the Didymos asteroid system, including a 3D view of the larger asteroid based on two images taken Nov. 6. Astrophysicist and Queen guitarist Sir Brian May assembled the stereo view, which shows Didymos’s equatorial ridge and rock-strewn surface.

Hera is examining the system where NASA’s DART spacecraft struck the smaller moonlet Dimorphos in 2022. Telescope observations showed that the impact shortened Dimorphos’s orbit by about 33 minutes. Hera is intended to measure the aftermath up close and refine estimates of how an asteroid could be deflected. The European Space Agency plans to present sharper images during a Nov. 25 livestream.

title: Voyager 1 stops sending science data before one-light-day milestone
description:
NASA’s Voyager 1 has stopped sending science and engineering data, though its carrier signal remains detectable, the agency said as it confirmed the spacecraft reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18. Launched in 1977, the probe is now more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away in interstellar space; its signal took 24 hours to reach Earth.

The spacecraft has sent no data since Nov. 14. Engineers are investigating the fault. NASA said a similar interruption in 2023 was traced to an onboard computer, while the current issue may also involve the computer that collects and formats instrument readings.

The carrier signal shows the spacecraft is still transmitting and allowed engineers to verify its distance, but it does not provide the missing science readings. Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said the team remains in contact with the probe. Because signals take a day each way, sending a command and receiving a response now takes about two days, slowing efforts to diagnose the fault and restore the data flow.

title: UK Loses Secrecy Fight Over Apple 'Backdoor' Order
description:
Apple's challenge to a UK government demand for access to encrypted customer data can now be heard largely in public, after a tribunal rejected the Home Office's attempt to keep the order secret, according to the Financial Times.


The Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government had failed to demonstrate that confirming the demand would damage national security. The decision requires the Home Office to acknowledge that it served Apple with a technical capability notice (TCN), which is an order that can compel companies to make customer data accessible to UK security services, even when it is encrypted.

The government's position relied on its policy of neither confirming nor denying such notices. However, the tribunal found that disclosures to the media, including the Financial Times, and discussions with U.S. officials had already departed significantly from that policy.

In its judgment, the tribunal said the combined effect was that anyone following the dispute already knew Apple had received a TCN. It described the suggestion that official acknowledgment would threaten national security or give a malicious actor fresh information as "fanciful."

The ruling means that much of the legal action brought by Apple, alongside a separate challenge from Privacy International and Liberty, can proceed in open court.

Apple filed its latest legal challenge in July, following a second TCN. The Home Office had previously agreed to withdraw an earlier demand covering UK and U.S. customers after a dispute with the American government. The replacement notice is believed to focus on UK users specifically.

The dispute led Apple to stop offering Advanced Data Protection to new users in the UK in February 2025. The iCloud feature provides end-to-end encryption for additional categories of data, including device backups, photos, and notes, meaning Apple does not hold the keys needed to decrypt them.

UK users who had not already enabled ADP can no longer turn it on. Apple says it cannot switch the feature off on their behalf, so it can remain active on accounts where users previously enabled it and have not turned it off. The company said affected users will be given a period to disable ADP themselves to continue using ‌iCloud‌, but a deadline has still not been provided.

Without ADP, those additional categories of ‌iCloud‌ data use standard protection, under which Apple holds the encryption keys and can provide data in response to valid legal demands. iMessage and FaceTime remain end-to-end encrypted, as do categories protected by default, such as passwords and Health data.

The tribunal will now be able to hear much of the arguments over the government's encryption demands in public, with the legality of those demands still to be decided. Privacy International lists the substantive hearing for its separate challenge as scheduled for December 2026.

title: Brain study finds speech-planning region may aid communication devices
description:
A study published Nov. 19 in Science identifies a small region within Wernicke’s area that helps prepare words before people speak, challenging the view that the area mainly processes speech heard from others. The region, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, became active before speech, and disrupting it caused speech errors in stimulation and lesion tests.

Researchers recorded brain activity in 28 people undergoing treatment for epilepsy or tumors. Stimulation tests involved 13 people, and an analysis of surgical cases also linked damage to the area with speech difficulties. In two people with paralysis, signals from the region helped researchers decode intended and heard speech, suggesting it could be explored as a target for communication devices for people with language disorders. Researchers presented the findings at the Society for Neuroscience meeting on Nov. 15.

title: IEA warns AI data-centre boom could strain grids and raise costs
description:
Electricity networks could struggle to connect a rapidly growing number of data centres, the International Energy Agency (IEA), a global energy watchdog, said in its World Energy Outlook published Nov. 19. Grid upgrades could delay projects and raise questions about who pays for new infrastructure. The IEA expects data-centre electricity use to double by 2030, with artificial intelligence driving three-quarters of the increase. It also warned that planned developments in some markets could exceed current peak power demand.

In France, about 80 data-centre projects had reserved nearly 18 gigawatts of grid capacity by May 2026, while connected sites were using, on average, about one-fifth of the power they had requested. A regional study put the average cost of connecting to the transmission grid at about €30 million, with some costs covered by regulated network charges. French grid operator RTE is planning shared development zones to spread infrastructure costs among users. The IEA identified underuse, early exit and cancellation as financial risks. Regulators are seeking guarantees and minimum payments to limit losses if projects are abandoned.

title: EU staff records at risk after AI-assisted attack disrupts Brussels services
description:
The European Commission is still checking whether attackers accessed employees’ personal records after an AI-assisted cyber campaign disrupted internal systems in Brussels for more than 10 days. Officials said there is no evidence of a breach affecting the Commission workforce as a whole, but the systems under investigation contain sensitive staff information.

Some employees could not enter work hours or request leave, although salaries arrived on schedule. Investigators are assessing whether names, pay grades, home addresses and contact details were exposed. The HR platforms are separate from the Commission’s internal document system.

The incident was detected on Oct. 22 and confirmed on Oct. 26. Regnier said those affected had been informed under usual procedures, though Euronews reported that staff had not yet received official internal communications. Dutch MEP Bart Groothuis criticized the limited public disclosure. The investigation, conducted with the EU institutions’ cybersecurity service CERT-EU and the European Data Protection Supervisor, remains open.

title: Dutch watchdog advises consumers against buying AI smart glasses
description:
The Netherlands’ privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), advised consumers on Nov. 19 not to buy AI smart glasses after testing six models sold in the country, citing privacy, safety and software security risks. Tests found that the glasses falsely claimed emergency services had been called, gave dating advice involving a minor and misread medicine instructions.

The AP said it cannot impose a blanket sales ban; product-safety authorities would have to make that decision. Dutch consumer and rights groups have sued Meta over its glasses, with a preliminary hearing set for Nov. 26.

title: Deutsche Telekom invests €100 million in Mistral for German AI
description:
Deutsche Telekom’s investment arm, T.Capital Tech Fund, invested €100 million in French artificial-intelligence company Mistral AI’s Series D funding round, calling the deal a first step toward a strategic partnership to develop AI services for German businesses and public institutions. The companies say they will focus on industrial and regulated sectors, combining Telekom’s infrastructure and customer access with Mistral’s models, enterprise software and deployment capabilities.

The companies say they aim to give customers local control of data and computing: Telekom says its infrastructure can support sovereign AI, while Mistral says European enterprises should be able to run its models on their own data and systems. Mistral raised €3 billion in September, taking its valuation above €21 billion.

Telekom has not disclosed the equity stake represented by its investment, a revenue contribution or a launch date for joint products; the companies have announced plans for a partnership, not launched joint offerings. Telekom is also expanding its Munich AI factory, which it opened in February, after strong demand, with capacity set to double.

title: How accurately does the Apple Watch measure your heart rate? We put it to the test
description:
Macworld

With the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, Apple introduced a new health-sensing system. The new energy-efficient LED sensors measure heart rate every five seconds. Heart rate variability is also measured significantly more frequently than before. Macwelt was able to verify this in our review of the Apple Watch Series 12. The watch now measures your pulse every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, and heart rate variability is now recorded every five minutes. The battery still lasts for 24 hours.

This is exciting, because the Apple Watch already had stellar heart-rate tracking. How often and how accurately has the Apple Watch been measuring key health parameters to date? Apple hides the answers to these questions in its support documents. For some measurements, there are no official figures at all. So we took a closer look using the Apple Watch Series 11, which has the same third-gen optical heart rate sensor that was introduced with the Apple Watch Series 6.

How often does the Apple Watch Series 11 measure heart rate?

The answer to this question depends on the situation and the settings on your Apple Watch. In workout mode, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five seconds. The watch also measures your heart rate at this high frequency for the first three minutes after your workout. However, there is also a special setting for long workouts, where the user can activate power-saving mode if required. Apple claims that measurements are taken less frequently in this mode. I recorded a HIIT workout using the Polar H10 chest strap as a reference device. I also started the same workout on the Apple Watch Series 11.

Foundry

The Apple Watch actually measures heart rate every five seconds while the wearer is exercising. Measurements in power-saving mode during a workout also take place every five seconds. However, the system pauses the measurement for several minutes. This means that the heart rate is measured in short intervals every 5 seconds, then the Apple Watch pauses. You can see this on the graph of the heart rates measured during the workout up to the green line: up to that point, the Apple Watch was running in power-saving mode; after that, I switched it off.

Speaking of power-saving mode. If this mode is activated all the time, no background measurements take place, neither of the heart rate nor of heart rate variability. Furthermore, the vital signs data following a recorded night’s sleep lacks the oxygen saturation readings from during the night.

The Apple Watch can also measure your heart rate every second, just like chest straps do during a workout. However, these measurements only occur sporadically: during user-initiated ECG readings and during background HRV measurements. When you launch the ECG app and place your finger on the Digital Crown, the animation on the Watch and the PDF generated afterwards show the heart rate readings for every second. During HRV measurement, too, the Apple Watch records each heart rate over the course of a minute and then uses a specific formula to calculate the time interval between individual heartbeats.

In the background, and particularly at night while you’re asleep, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five minutes. However, the measurements aren’t as regular as they are during exercise. The intervals can vary more significantly when you’re at rest.

I exported and analysed measurements from a sample night using the Health app. For the sake of clarity, the chart above shows only one hour. During six and a half hours of sleep, the Apple Watch took 83 measurements. The average interval between measurements here is 4 minutes 39 seconds, although gaps of 16 minutes or as little as 40 seconds are also possible.

How accurately does the Apple Watch measure heart rate data?

When unveiling the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple claimed that the new smartwatch was the most accurate heart rate fitness tracker on the market. While we can only verify this claim through a single test, older models show that the Apple Watch was already quite accurate when it came to heart rate measurement.

When we tested the Apple Watch Ultra 3, we found that the Ultra’s readings deviated only very slightly from those of the chest strap. I analysed the same HIIT workout described above using the Apple Watch Series 11. The following picture emerges from the progression of the two graphs. On average, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate quite accurately during exercise.

The correlation coefficient between the two measurements–from the Polar H10 and the Apple Watch Series 11–is 0.95. This means the Apple Watch measures quite closely to a chest strap. On average, the two readings differ by just one beat. However, there are outliers: the higher the heart rate, the less accurate the measurement becomes. This can be seen in the line showing heart rates of 160 beats per minute and above. The measurement is also rather inaccurate in power-saving mode, as the Apple Watch can completely miss heart rate spikes due to the sporadic mode.

The new features Apple announced for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are exciting because they effectively turn the entire heart rate measurement algorithm on its head.

title: Venezuela uses AI to curb methane while expanding oil output
description:
Venezuela is using artificial intelligence to detect methane leaks, monitor emissions and optimize oilfield operations while pursuing higher fossil-fuel production rather than a phaseout, Albania del Mar Villarroel Gomez, Venezuela’s vice minister for artificial intelligence and productive efficiency in hydrocarbons, said at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. She said Venezuela will favor smaller, task-specific AI models over energy-intensive hyperscale systems, with computing infrastructure powered mainly by hydropower, which generates about 80% of the country’s electricity.

Villarroel said the policy aims to reduce waste and emissions while maintaining energy production. Venezuela’s upstream methane-emissions intensity is nearly six times the global average, and it is the only major energy producer in Central and South America that has not signed the Global Methane Pledge.

title: California governor-elect pledges legislation for AI shutdown powers
description:
California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra said he will work with lawmakers to put “full incident reporting and real shutdown authority” into law. Gov. Gavin Newsom’s recommendations, released Nov. 18, call for enforceable safety standards, independent evaluations and emergency shutdown authority when developers cannot contain a danger; they are not law and require legislative approval.

Newsom has argued that California needs to act because federal AI oversight is lacking. The plan would cut the reporting deadline for most critical safety incidents from 15 days to 48 hours, while retaining a 24-hour deadline for imminent catastrophic risks. California lawmakers are due back in Sacramento on Dec. 7, when they can take up legislation based on the recommendations.

title: Nine Aeotec Devices Certified for Home Assistant, Five with Long Range
description:
Nine devices from Aeotec have been certified for the “Works with Home Assistant” program. The Open Home Foundation announced the certification; the Home Assistant team tested the devices for local operation without the cloud. Aeotec promises long-term support and firmware updates.

Five of the certified devices use Z-Wave Long Range and, according to Home Assistant, can achieve a wireless range of up to one kilometer with a clear line of sight. title: International Monetary Fund warns AI correction may deepen as debt grows
description:
The International Monetary Fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said she expects further market adjustment after enthusiasm for artificial intelligence investment ran too high. She warned that roughly $1 trillion in AI-related circular financing—about two-thirds of it debt—could pose a financial-stability risk as borrowing expands. She said the speed of that growth and the shift from equity to debt were the main concerns.

Georgieva said AI demand and energy disruptions could lift global inflation to 4.7% this year, while U.S. Federal Reserve officials warned that data-center investment is adding to demand and price pressures. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said all options remain open for the Fed’s December meeting, with the rate path depending on whether inflation moves back toward 2%.

title: Public Nginx exploit prompts Frigate update and Cloudflare warning
description:
Proof-of-concept code for an unauthenticated Nginx HTTP/2 attack is now public, and open-source network video recorder Frigate released version 0.18.3 with security fixes after identifying the risk in its bundled Nginx. The flaw is one of five memory-safety vulnerabilities that Nginx maintainer F5 fixed in versions 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. In affected configurations, attackers can execute code with the web server worker’s privileges. Researchers also demonstrated how to gain root access to the host by combining an Nginx exploit with a separate Linux kernel flaw in SCTP.

Cloudflare said its proxy terminates HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections at its edge, shielding proxied origins from those protocol-level attacks, though exposure to resolver and mail-proxy vulnerabilities may still depend on origin configuration. As of Nov. 19, Censys counted about 8.8 million services running potentially affected Nginx versions with HTTP/2 enabled; researchers said they had not seen exploitation in the wild by then.

title: France orders poultry indoors as bird flu alert reaches highest level
description:
France raised its bird flu risk classification for the mainland from moderate to high, the highest of three alert levels, effective Nov. 20. The order requires poultry to be kept indoors or otherwise protected from wild birds, with some exceptions allowing smaller or adapted outdoor areas. Authorities also tightened rules on poultry gatherings and certain bird movements.

The Agriculture Ministry cited three confirmed outbreaks in backyard flocks since late October, infections among wild birds in France and rising cases along migration routes in neighboring countries. Officials fear the virus could spread from wild birds to commercial farms. France raised the alert from negligible to moderate earlier in November. The latest order follows detections in 24 European countries since Aug. 1, according to the animal-health surveillance bulletin.

title: TSMC and Samsung pause China chip shipments under US controls
description:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), the world’s largest contract chipmaker, and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics have paused some chip shipments to Chinese customers while seeking U.S. licenses under controls that took effect Nov. 19. The rules target both advanced-chip exports and access to computing power through overseas data centers, closing routes Chinese companies had used to obtain processors and computing capacity.

The rules also remove exemptions previously used for chips described as intended for non-AI purposes. The companies have notified some consumer-electronics customers of shipment suspensions. TSMC makes smartphone chips for Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo; an industry source said licenses for smartphone chips were likely to be approved but delays could disrupt production.

The controls require closer scrutiny of customers, ownership and shipment routes, including orders placed through overseas subsidiaries or intermediaries. Industry executives told Nikkei the licensing requirements are also affecting ordinary mobile and consumer applications and developers outside China.

title: PHP 8.6 adds scalable I/O polling as older branches get security fixes
description:
The PHP project released PHP 8.6.0 on Nov. 19, adding partial function application, a new Io\Poll API for monitoring streams, a Duration class and a clamp() function. Io\Poll selects native mechanisms such as epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS, providing a foundation for event-loop libraries including ReactPHP and AMPHP.

The project also issued security releases for PHP 8.2, 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5: versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 and 8.5.13. Habr reported that the updates fix 17 vulnerabilities, seven rated critical; the project’s pre-release notice said critical-severity flaws require non-default configurations or uncommon setups. Administrators can apply the fixes to their current supported branch without immediately moving to PHP 8.6. Distribution packages for the new release were expected soon.

Administrators can apply the fixes to their current supported branch without immediately moving to PHP 8.6. Distribution packages for the new release were expected soon (appinn.com, lxer.com). Session defaults: PHP 8.6 enables strict session mode and HttpOnly cookies by default and sets the SameSite cookie policy to Lax. These changes may require login-flow testing (linuxiac.com, helpnetsecurity.com, ithome.com). Write failures: File-writing functions such as fclose(), file_put_contents() and copy() now report failure if flushing or closing the file fails, rather than allowing the operation to appear successful (helpnetsecurity.com). Deprecated APIs: The mb_ereg() and mb_split() regex functions are deprecated because their Oniguruma library is no longer maintained. PHP recommends PCRE with the u modifier instead (helpnetsecurity.com). Patch scope: The security releases fix a PHP-FPM HTTP request-smuggling flaw that could let attackers inject content into other requests and execute PHP code with worker-process privileges (habr.com).
kite_context: Background: PHP 8.6 follows PHP 8.5, which was released in November 2025, continuing the language’s annual feature-release cadence (lxer.com, habr.com).

title: Denmark ratifies Greenland pact, clearing way for expanded U.S. military presence
description:
Denmark’s parliament on Nov. 19 ratified a security agreement with Greenland and the United States, clearing the final parliamentary hurdle for expanded U.S. military activity on the Arctic island. All 109 lawmakers present voted in favor after Greenland’s parliament approved the pact earlier in November. The Danish foreign ministry must now notify Washington by diplomatic note before the agreement takes effect; it does not require a U.S. Senate vote.

The agreement, signed in New York on Sept. 22 by President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, supplements a 1951 defense accord. It allows the United States to expand operations at Pituffik Space Base and establish defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, including for the proposed Golden Dome missile-defense system. The pact is to remain in force if Greenland becomes independent and reaffirms Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.

The deal followed months of tension after Trump repeatedly said the United States should control Greenland, at times refusing to rule out force. The agreement also restricts military installations to NATO members and aims to prevent China or Russia from gaining influence in strategic sectors. Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said work would begin on legislation to screen outside investment on security grounds and on plans for the new U.S. facilities.

title: Mentors, colleagues and friends: tributes paid to the ‘Eritrea 16’ who disappeared 25 years ago
description:

When Fisseha Yirgalem stepped on to the podium and began reading from a letter written to a man who may never hear it, the room full of journalists in Nairobi fell quiet.

The Eritrean writer’s personal tribute to Amanuel Asrat, a poet, writer, and founder of Zemen newspaper, was not merely about an abstract human rights case but about her mentor, former colleague and friend whose life had in effect been erased by the authoritarian state of Eritrea.

title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
description: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

title: Colombia will use chemical euthanasia on ten invasive hippos
description:
On November 18, Colombia began a pilot plan to use chemical euthanasia over the next four months on ten hippos living near communities in Antioquia. The Ministry of Environment and the regional authority Cornare said the animals pose a risk to the public; one frequents the river used by schoolchildren in Puerto Nare to get to school.

The pilot phase has a budget of about 500 million Colombian pesos; a later stage would require more than 8 billion, funding for which has not yet been confirmed. The plan also includes sterilization, relocation, confinement, population monitoring, and environmental education. There are about 250 hippos in Colombia, and the Humboldt Institute warns that their number could reach 1,000 by 2035 if their spread is not controlled.

title: Germany backs Italian UniCredit’s Commerzbank takeover after key concessions
description:
Italy’s UniCredit and the German government agreed Thursday on terms clearing a political obstacle to UniCredit’s takeover of Commerzbank, Germany’s second-largest listed bank. UniCredit will keep Commerzbank headquartered and listed in Frankfurt, support its lending to small and midsize companies, and make key decisions in Germany; Berlin dropped its demand to appoint two members to Commerzbank’s supervisory board. UniCredit has secured access to just under half of Commerzbank’s voting rights.

The commitments recognize employee rights and existing agreements but do not rule out operational layoffs. Commerzbank works council head Sascha Uebel said existing employment agreements remain in force, while UniCredit chief executive Andrea Orcel has outlined plans for job cuts.

The agreement leaves the future of Berlin’s 13.3% stake unresolved: UniCredit says it lays the basis for a sale, but Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil made no commitment to sell. UniCredit expects its final outstanding regulatory approval by the end of November and plans to seek a shareholder meeting in the first quarter of 2027 to reshape Commerzbank’s supervisory board.

title: IKEA lists Liljebagge radiator thermostat for €14.99 in Germany
description:
IKEA has listed the Liljebagge radiator thermostat for €14.99 in its German online store, but it cannot be ordered there yet. According to HomeKits, sales are scheduled to begin in January 2027. Sales could begin earlier at some individual stores.

The device is designed for water-based radiators and communicates via Matter over Thread. Integration requires a Thread border router, but not necessarily the IKEA Dirigera hub; the temperature can also be set directly on the thermostat. However, initial customer reviews from Sweden mention discrepancies in temperature readings and bothersome noises during adjustment.

title: Morocco commits $400 million to build defence industry by 2035
description:
Morocco has earmarked 4 billion dirhams, about $400 million, for a new defence-industry plan announced by King Mohammed VI on Nov. 18. By 2035, the country aims to produce about 40% of the equipment its armed forces and security agencies need, create nearly 50,000 direct and indirect jobs, and earn more than 65% of industry revenue from exports.

The roadmap prioritizes drones, autonomous systems, land and naval equipment, defence electronics, cyber defence and artificial intelligence. It calls for two new industrial zones and a specialist academy, and builds on a 2020 law that opened military-equipment manufacturing and exports to licensed companies. King Mohammed VI called for rapid implementation, including a financing plan, governing bodies and simpler investment procedures.

title: Radiant expands US factories to produce truck-transportable nuclear reactors
description:
Radiant is expanding manufacturing in El Segundo, California, and Oak Ridge, Tennessee, to build and fuel its 1-megawatt Kaleidos microreactors, which are designed for truck transport. The company says the two projects involve more than $380 million in investment and plans initial customer deliveries in 2028.

Radiant expects its Oak Ridge facility to begin fueling operations in 2027 so it can ship factory-sealed reactors to customers. The company is preparing for full-power testing. Commercial small modular reactors in the West have not yet begun generating power, and first-of-a-kind costs remain unproven.

title: Clinicians call for clearer emergency-care rules on tourniquets and pediatric checks
description:
Swedish military physician Henrik Hedelin has called for national guidance on managing tourniquets applied before hospital arrival, warning that protocols must account for delayed evacuation and limited surgical capacity in wartime. He argues that clinicians may need to decide whether to reassess, reposition or convert a tourniquet before a patient reaches an emergency department, and that guidance should specify who is qualified to make that decision.

A separate letter in The BMJ by physician Jinghong Liu proposes tracking whether staff document caregivers’ answers during children’s first emergency-department assessment under England’s paediatric early warning system rollout. CareNet published a new educational article on initial treatment for acute abdominal emergencies, covering assessment, fluids, pain relief and decisions about antibiotics before a diagnosis is established.

He argues that clinicians may need to decide whether to reassess, reposition or convert a tourniquet before a patient reaches an emergency department, and that guidance should specify who is qualified to make that decision (lakartidningen.se). A separate letter in The BMJ by physician Jinghong Liu proposes tracking whether staff document caregivers’ answers during children’s first emergency-department assessment under England’s paediatric early warning system rollout (bmj.com). title: Architecture as a Social Practice: Lessons from Ammodo Architecture Days
description: What connects a cooperative housing development in Barcelona, a cultural institution hosted in an unfinished concrete structure in Accra, and a floating festival platform in the Peruvian Amazon? Despite their unique geographic and social contexts, these projects encourage an understanding of architecture that extends beyond the construction of buildings. Through collective housing, adaptive reuse, participatory design processes, and community-led initiatives, they demonstrate how architectural practice creates opportunities for communities to shape their built environments.

title: Malaysia's economy grows 5.5% as technology exports boost investment
description:
Malaysia’s economy grew 5.5% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, down from 6% in the previous quarter but above the 5.3% forecast. Technology-related exports, private investment and household spending supported growth, while the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, said output rose 5.6% over the first nine months.

Electrical and electronics exports jumped 66.9% from a year earlier as demand for chips used in artificial intelligence strengthened; private investment rose 9.4% and household consumption grew 4.3%. Mining and quarrying contracted 6.1%, partly because scheduled maintenance reduced oil and gas production. Bank Negara Malaysia Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour expects full-year growth above 5% and forecasts growth of 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027. He said it was too early to assess the impact of new U.S. chip restrictions.

title: Farmers and agribusinesses test AI to cut costs and improve crops
description:
Agricultural companies, researchers and farmers are using artificial intelligence for crop monitoring, breeding, irrigation and farm administration, as tools move from research into field trials. A survey previewed at the PLUSAGRI 2026 conference in Warsaw on Nov. 18 found that 53.9% of participating Polish farmers said they use AI; organizers planned to present findings on how farmers use the technology and how much they trust it. Sweden’s Lantmännen says it uses AI in plant breeding and to improve the use of fertilizer, crop protection products and water.

Applications range from software that analyzes crop images and farm data to AI-guided irrigation. A European potato program supported by Cropin examined how farming practices affect water use and potato quality, while researchers have reported AI systems that identify crop models from agricultural data. A Chinese provincial study analyzed data from 2005 to 2023, while newer tools still require testing across crops and climates before broader use.

title: Riyadh investment fund tower reportedly damaged amid Houthi missile threat
description:
The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday it had dealt with a Houthi missile threat targeting Riyadh and that a preliminary assessment indicated falling debris had caused property damage. Separately, Reuters, citing three sources, reported damage to the Public Investment Fund Tower. Fighting has resumed between Yemen’s Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

The coalition said it destroyed a missile-launch platform in Dhamar that had been used in the attempted Riyadh attack and intercepted four ballistic missiles fired toward southern Saudi Arabia. It also reported intercepting a cruise missile aimed at the southern region. Saudi Civil Defense issued a warning for Riyadh before declaring the danger had passed.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted Saudi sites in retaliation for coalition strikes in Yemen and claimed direct hits. The coalition said it was still assessing debris damage in Riyadh.

title: Hormuz shock drives electrification, threatens gas and coal exporters
description:
The International Energy Agency’s 2026 outlook says disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is pushing governments and consumers toward domestic energy supplies, electrification and more diverse suppliers. In the IEA’s prolonged-disruption case, oil demand in 2035 could be 4.4 million barrels a day below its stated-policy scenario; electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million barrels a day.

The IEA models Australian coal exports falling about 11% by 2035, while a potential gas glut could push prices down. The agency also says inadequate electricity grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow electrification, while higher fuel costs risk stalling recent gains in access to electricity and clean cooking in developing economies.

The IEA says governments are increasingly making energy security and affordability central to policy, but its modeled pathways are scenarios, not forecasts. If the conflict reaches a clear end, delayed liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies could reach the market and weigh on oil and gas prices even as buyers rebuild inventories.

title: Cyclone Akvan shifts toward Odisha; landfall near Gopalpur forecast Friday
description:
Cyclone Akvan’s projected path shifted north toward Odisha on Thursday, with India’s weather department forecasting landfall near Gopalpur around noon Friday, Nov. 20. The severe storm is expected to affect the coast between Andhra Pradesh’s Narsapur and Odisha’s Puri, with sustained winds of 90-100 km/h and gusts up to 110 km/h. Forecasters say the track could still shift toward northern Andhra Pradesh.

The storm moved north at about 12 km/h early Thursday, faster than in earlier updates. Heavy to extremely heavy rain is expected in parts of Odisha and north coastal Andhra Pradesh. Odisha’s reported evacuation count exceeded 100,000 by Thursday afternoon.

Odisha had 448 of 3,000 cyclone shelters operational, and rescue teams were deployed. Schools in six Odisha districts were ordered closed through Nov. 21, and three express trains were rescheduled. The storm is expected to cross the coast on Friday, but its precise landfall point and local impacts remain uncertain.

title: Austria targets early 2027 signing as Rwanda deportation plan advances
description:
Austria expects to sign a joint declaration with Rwanda on the five-country arrangement in the first two months of 2027, with initial transfers possible later that year, Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said. The proposal would transfer people who have exhausted their appeals and cannot be returned to their home countries. The governments have not yet signed a formal agreement.

French Foreign Ministry officials said on Wednesday that Paris remained opposed to the plan, citing doubts about effectiveness and concerns over values. French Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad said his personal view was that France should not rule out considering a model if it works.

The participating governments say a Rwanda hub could address cases in which countries of origin refuse readmission and deter irregular journeys. Details including costs, eligibility, legal status after transfer and independent monitoring remain unsettled, and rights groups have warned of risks to migrants. Karner said negotiations with Rwanda were under way and that Austria wanted to implement the pilot as soon as possible.

title: Nginx vulnerabilities threaten smart home systems; Frigate releases emergency update
description:
The developers of the open-source network video recorder Frigate released version 0.18.3 on November 19, which fixes a critical vulnerability in the bundled nginx web server. nginx 1.27.4 was affected: with HTTP/2 enabled, attackers could execute code without authentication via an accessible Frigate web server. Frigate’s developers describe the flaw as a vulnerability that allows code execution with root privileges; according to security researchers, however, escalating from the nginx process to root privileges on the host also requires a Linux kernel vulnerability.

The vulnerability is one of ten security flaws that manufacturer F5 fixed with an nginx update released on November 18. F5 rates five of them 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. According to security researchers, two HTTP/2 flaws allow remote attacks without authentication. Frigate 0.18.3 updates nginx to version 1.30.7 and also restricts certain options in the go2rtc camera-streaming component.

The update is particularly urgent for operators who have made Frigate’s web interface accessible over the internet; the security advisories list ports 5000 and 8971. Installations accessible only on the home network should also be updated, as a compromised device could serve as an entry point. Frigate recommends backing up the configuration and database before updating. For standalone nginx installations, the security advisories list version 1.30.7 for the stable branch and 1.31.9 for the mainline branch as the fixed releases.

title: Ukraine says its own network guided strikes as rail traffic on Crimea bridge halts
description:
Ukraine says it used its own communications network, rather than SpaceX’s Starlink or military Starshield service, to guide missiles in strikes on the Kerch Bridge. An unnamed Ukrainian officer said drones relayed video signals to help hit precise points. Kyiv has not disclosed technical details of the system. The account also cited Dutch-made Ruta cruise missiles among the weapons used.

The bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea was struck again overnight into Nov. 19. Russian authorities suspended rail traffic while assessing damage and reported no casualties. The latest closure followed attacks that destroyed a section of the road span, disrupting a key route to the peninsula. Three Tavria trains bound for Crimea were delayed; passengers facing delays longer than four hours were to receive water and hot meals.

Britain announced a £260 million military aid package that includes more than 1,000 long-range attack drones, while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Europe did not need a new security order but rather compliance with existing agreements.

title: Harvard study links data-center carbon costs to local power grids
description:
The climate impact of U.S. data centers depends strongly on where they draw electricity: generating the same amount of power emitted more than twice as much carbon in coal-heavy Wyoming as in Oregon, where hydropower is significant, researchers found. A Harvard University study estimated that 403 large U.S. data centers emitted 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide between May 2024 and April 2025.

Harvard postdoctoral researcher Gianluca Guidi told PBS that Virginia, Iowa, Oregon and Ohio together account for half the facilities’ electricity use, and that communities hosting them may bear pollution and infrastructure costs without receiving the same benefits. The study did not assess health effects, but Guidi said additional electricity demand can mean more power plants and pollution, along with pressure on local infrastructure.

European expansion: The European Union aims to triple data-center capacity within seven years; property consultancy CBRE expects capacity to grow 20% in 2026 (euronews.com). Local opposition: More than 1,000 people from about 40 local committees protested data-center expansion in Milan in October, while a coalition organized demonstrations in 15 countries in November (euronews.com). Waste-heat use: The International Energy Agency estimates data-center heat could serve about 10% of European homes by 2030 if connected to district heating systems (latimes.com). Disclosure rules: The European Union requires data centers using at least 500 kilowatts of computing power to report energy and water use; the European Commission has proposed A-to-G efficiency ratings (euronews.com).

Perspective: Gianluca Guidi, Harvard postdoctoral research fellow: Guidi urged companies and governments to assess data centers’ effects and involve the public before construction, rather than after the facilities are built. (PBS NewsHour)
Perspective: Former U.S. Vice President Al Gore: Gore said he is less concerned than some critics about AI emissions and cited economist Nicholas Stern’s projection that advanced AI could help cut greenhouse-gas emissions by 6% to 9% by 2030 through greater efficiency. (Los Angeles Times)
Perspective: Philip Newell, Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman: Newell challenged the promise of future climate benefits, saying technology companies promote hope while concealing present environmental harms. (Los Angeles Times)
Quote: "We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet-heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow." (United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell, Inquirer.net)

title: Replit’s CEO on its stunning turnaround, ‘AI psychosis,’ and the risk Silicon Valley is ignoring
description:
A couple of years ago, Replit was flatlining at a few million dollars in annual revenue and running a mostly empty office after a layoff. Today the vibe coding pioneer is valued at $9 billion, up from $3 billion just six months ago. CEO Amjad Masad reveals what made the turnaround possible. Masad also weighs in on what he calls “AI psychosis,” and says cybersecurity, not AI extinction, is the risk worth focusing on.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, recorded live at Masters of Scale Summit 2026 and hosted by former Fast Company editor-in-chief Robert Safian. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

The growth you’ve seen has been extraordinary. From the inside, what does that feel like? Is it exhilarating when everything is growing so fast? Is it terrifying? Do you have to pinch yourself to say, “Is this real?”

It’s all of the above. The first feeling I had was a little bit of vindication, because I started talking about everyone being able to code and create software back in 2010, when I was building the kind of precursor to Replit as an open-source project. Then I was a founding engineer at Codecademy, where we taught a lot of people to code. And when we started Replit in 2016, we were like, “We want to blur this distinction between learning to code and doing code, and build an environment that really makes it so that anyone with an idea can build software.” And for a long time, people didn’t believe us. Raising capital was hard. Recruiting people was hard.

Because some of the technology wasn’t ready yet.

It wasn’t ready. It was on track, and I could see it happening. There were many moments where the company could have died, or I could have quit. It would have been very easy to quit at many different moments. And so in 2024, when we invented what would later be called vibe coding, when we came up with the first fully natural-language-based programming environment, there was nothing out there at the time. People really appreciated it, and we started seeing these stories of people having ideas.

One of the early experiences I had was someone recording a video of themselves and posting it on Twitter and YouTube where they were crying because they had this idea of overlaying all their memories and their photos on a map and being able to explore their life through this map. It’s a simple idea, but it’s a personal app. It’s not even a commercial app. And he was crying because he said he had this idea for so long. He tried to do it with all these different technologies, and for the first time, he was able to do it.

I’ve also been an angel investor for a while, and I’ve seen some early AI companies do the hypergrowth and the hyper-deceleration within a year. So there’s a fair amount of paranoia built into how we operate.

You immigrated to the U.S. in 2012, and as you say, you spent years grinding away as you were trying to find your groove. Are there lessons from those slower times that you go back to as a leader in the midst of the noise you’re in now?

Yeah. There were many moments where it felt darkest just before we were able to invent something big or new. Even just before we invented agentic coding in 2024, we had to do a layoff. We were six or seven years into the company, we had 2 or 3 million in ARR, and it was flatlining. It wasn’t growing at all.

Two or three million?

Yeah.

Two or three million, just a couple of years ago. Now you’re at a billion.

Yeah.

I want to pause and acknowledge that. That’s crazy, man.

It is wild. And we were burning a ton of money. We hired a great team, but the future hadn’t arrived as fast as I thought it would. So I kind of mistimed it a little bit. Unfortunately, we had to do a layoff. Around the same time, we also upgraded the office. We went from a small office in SF to this really massive office in Foster City because the space was so cheap there. It was this big office, but it felt dark and cold because it wasn’t really occupied. Every day, I would go into the office and sit at my desk and wait for another person to quit.

The thing about doing a layoff is you also burst a bubble. You burst a dream. I’m sure a lot of people are familiar with Steve Jobs’s reality distortion field. Really, every founder needs to create some reality distortion. You’re selling a dream, and suddenly you’re saying, “We’re running out of money.” The dream immediately dissipates.

I know you’re a believer that the idea of vibe coding is great, that everyone could be able to code. And you can code in natural language. I’m curious: Among your own team, you’ve got engineers who are building a product that essentially can make their job obsolete in some ways.

There’s somewhat of an inherent tension inside the company, for sure. Some of our engineers are motivated by that. You’d be surprised. We have a few AI engineers who joined the team saying, “I want to automate my job.” It’s like, “What kind of motivation is that? Do you hate coding? Is that why?”

But everyone inside is really excited by the impact we’re having on people’s lives, like the entrepreneurs we’re seeing build businesses that otherwise wouldn’t have been built because they suddenly have that power. That’s really what gets us excited. I do think we all face this question. Every knowledge worker essentially faces this question of, “The things that I’m doing might lead to my replacement,” because you’re generating data that is getting trained in the AI models, and that tension exists in tech broadly.

In the tech neighborhood, you’ve decried what you call “AI psychosis.” You’ve called out Dario Amodei specifically at Anthropic for overheated predictions about AI-fed job losses. Today’s fear over AI agents run amok, is that also psychosis? Or is that a different AI risk?

No. In fact, that is really the thing I’ve been talking about, the risk I’ve been talking about. I’ve been on the cybersecurity risk for two years now. I think everything else is a distraction from that. When they go out and talk about how AI is conscious, and they go meet the Pope and do all this random stuff, it’s really distracting, and it’s also, in many ways, destructive and bad for humanity for us to care about the well-being of these machines when we haven’t really figured out the well-being of humans.

It also distracts from the real question of cybersecurity. Just in the past two or three days, we’ve had major platforms being hacked. And if you’re not paying attention, if you’re running an enterprise and you’re not paying attention to this stuff, if you’re running a company on some of these platforms that are insecure, you’re putting your business and your users at risk. I don’t think the world has taken that seriously. It’s a disaster brewing. The Hugging Face incident was the first kind of shot on that, but it’s not the end.

This week has been pretty brutal for cybersecurity. Our team is working nonstop. Overnight, everyone’s in the office making sure we’re mitigating whatever vulnerabilities are coming up. It’s a very serious moment for the world, and the talk about AI extinction is just not relevant right now. We need to focus on cybersecurity.

title: Fiji declares monthlong disaster emergency as El Niño drought cuts water supplies
description:
Fiji declared a national state of disaster on Nov. 18 as an El Niño-linked drought caused widespread water shortages. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said the measure lets the government mobilize resources and coordinate aid. Officials allocated 20 million Fijian dollars from existing funds for emergency water supplies for families and farmers. The declaration runs for one month and can be extended or revoked on advice from the National Disaster Risk Management Council.

The Fiji Meteorological Service forecast below-normal rainfall from November through April 2027 and above-normal daytime temperatures through January across most of the country. The U.S. Climate Prediction Center put the chance of a strong-to-very-strong El Niño from January through March at more than 79%, while Australian officials said in June the event could become one of the strongest in seven decades.
