title: Japan PM and China's Xi shake hands at APEC without formal talks
description:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Chinese President Xi Jinping shook hands at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 18 and again on Nov. 19, but held no formal bilateral meeting. During the second encounter, Takaichi spoke to Xi for about 10 seconds; he nodded but did not reply, Japanese media reported.

The encounters were the leaders’ first face-to-face contact in about a year. In November 2025, Takaichi told parliament that a Taiwan crisis could threaten Japan’s survival and potentially warrant a response by its Self-Defense Forces. Beijing demanded that she retract the remarks and imposed measures including rare-earth export restrictions; Tokyo says its position on Taiwan has not changed.

Takaichi also met Russian President Vladimir Putin for about 30 minutes on Nov. 18. Japan sought to convey its concerns to U.S. President Donald Trump before his planned trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin, and was arranging a call with Trump afterward. Takaichi was scheduled to hold a news conference and leave China on Nov. 19.

title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
description:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

title: Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi presses Putin over detained reporter, seized assets
description:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin for about 30 minutes after an APEC welcome dinner in Shenzhen on Nov. 18, the first face-to-face meeting between Japanese and Russian leaders since 2019. Japan said Takaichi raised the detention of Hokkaido Shimbun reporter Yuki Imai and the protection of Japanese companies. The leaders agreed to continue communicating at various levels.

Japanese sources said Takaichi called for Imai’s immediate release and urged Moscow to reverse its temporary takeover of Japan Tobacco assets in Russia. Imai was arrested in Sakhalin on Oct. 13 on suspicion of espionage. His current detention period is due to expire Dec. 12 but could be extended.

Japan had protested a day earlier after suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace. The countries also disagree over Ukraine and sovereignty over disputed islands. Russia’s Presidential Executive Office had not publicly confirmed the conversation.

title: Carney keeps Canada trade options open after brief Trump meeting
description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump met for just under 20 minutes in Shenzhen on Nov. 18. Their offices said they would continue working toward a trade agreement. The meeting was not on Carney’s public itinerary. Carney said Canada could not simply wait for Washington and was pursuing other markets.

At a parliamentary hearing, Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc defended Carney’s account of why talks broke down in August, which U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had disputed. Canada’s chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, told MPs the government must prepare for an arrangement that may not be tariff-free.

Carney has pointed to agreements with Southeast Asian partners and the Philippines and said Canada expects to sign a trade deal with India in the coming months. He has also defended trade diversification as protection against overdependence on any single partner.

title: European allies meet in Berlin as Trump and Putin discuss Ukraine
description:
European leaders and Ukrainian officials are meeting U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Berlin on Thursday as European governments seek a role in U.S.-led efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine. The Coalition of the Willing gathering includes the leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy, as well as NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

German officials said the discussions would cover legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine after a ceasefire, economic recovery and preparations for another round of multilateral negotiations. The meeting coincides with President Donald Trump’s talks in Shenzhen with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. European officials are concerned that decisions affecting Ukraine and Europe could be made without them.

Last week’s U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi—the first involving Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. officials in nine months—produced no breakthrough on ending the war, though the sides agreed to a prisoner exchange. Russia is seeking Ukraine’s Donbas region, while Kyiv opposes giving up territory. European allies say the Berlin meeting will let them respond quickly to developments in China. EU leaders are due to discuss a proposed Ukraine loan in Brussels next week.

title: Southeast Asian governments assess U.S. chip controls as rule takes effect
description:
Southeast Asian governments are seeking clarity and preparing support as U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips take effect, targeting shipments to five destinations and Chinese companies’ access to remote computing. The rules require licenses for certain chip exports, re-exports and transfers to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, and cover data centers supplying large volumes of computing power to companies in China and other restricted countries.

Indonesia said it is reviewing the rules with industry and wants technical talks with Washington. Malaysia is seeking details on licensing and data-center services, while Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani said operators must comply with U.S. requirements. Thailand’s Commerce Ministry said it would coordinate with other agencies and provide affected businesses with information and support.

The controls could complicate investment decisions and operations in a region where demand from Chinese technology companies has helped drive data-center growth. Indonesia is developing a framework to support legitimate trade and reduce diversion risks; Malaysia plans to notify its 117 approved data-center projects once Washington communicates the requirements.

title: Chinese fossils extend Homo erectus survival and reveal rainforest adaptation
description:
Two studies published in Nature on Nov. 18 report that Homo erectus lived in southern China far later than previously documented and inhabited tropical rainforest there. Nine fossil teeth from Naxian and Baxian caves in Guangxi date to 324,000–184,000 years ago. Researchers identified eight as Homo erectus, extending its known mainland Asian record by roughly 200,000 years.

A ninth tooth, PA1796, does not match Homo erectus, Neanderthals or modern humans. Researchers cannot yet tell whether it belonged to a Denisovan or another hominin. Its presence suggests at least two human groups inhabited the region during the period represented by the finds.

Chemical evidence from the teeth and animal fossils indicates that the Homo erectus individuals lived in a rainforest ecosystem, challenging the idea that only Homo sapiens could use such habitats. Strontium signatures also suggest some individuals moved across a wide area as children. Researchers continue searching southern China’s caves for fossils that could help identify the mystery tooth and clarify the species’ history.

title: South Korea adds AI-cheating checks as 551,864 take college exam
description:
South Korea held its annual College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), known as Suneung, on Thursday, Nov. 19, for 551,864 applicants at 1,312 centers. Authorities tightened security after the top scorer on a national tax-accountant exam admitted using artificial intelligence to cheat. Officials checked glasses for concealed cameras, covered clothing buttons with stickers, restricted test-takers to approved pencils and sent emergency phone alerts. Authorities deployed about 75,000 proctors and 8,400 additional staff.

The first alert revealed that 22 students were carrying smartphones in nine cities and provinces; the Education Ministry said it had not confirmed the presence of other advanced devices among those students. Separately, proctors at a test center in Yongin found a miniature camera and an earphone, and local education officials were examining whether they had been used. Authorities said the phone checks did not delay the exam’s start.

Also on Thursday, Seoul National University dentistry student Lee Jin-woo, who faced allegations of using AI to achieve a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test, was found in cardiac arrest at a motel after missing a planned livestream to demonstrate his test-taking ability. Yonhap later reported that Lee had died. He had denied cheating, and police were investigating complaints filed by two lawyers. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook separately ordered officials to preserve last year’s CSAT papers.

title: California Gov. Newsom proposes emergency shutdown powers for risky AI
description:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom released recommendations on Nov. 18 that would require baseline safety standards and ongoing independent checks for powerful AI systems and allow state officials to order emergency shutdowns when developers cannot contain a danger. The proposals also call for state authority to limit recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems help design their successors. Newsom presented the plan as a response to what he says is a lack of federal oversight. The recommendations are not law and would require legislative action.

The report proposes shortening the deadline for most critical-incident reports from 15 days to 48 hours, adding a channel for reporting near misses and extending whistleblower protections to former employees and contractors. It also recommends requiring companies to report how much of their AI research and development they automate and funding public computing capacity for independent safety research.

California lawmakers return to Sacramento on Dec. 7. Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra said he intends to work with them on standards, independent verification, incident reporting and shutdown authority.

title: Miami jury convicts Haitian-American pastor in Moïse assassination plot
description:
A federal jury in Miami convicted Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a Haitian-American pastor, on all eight charges tied to the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse, including conspiring to kill or kidnap someone outside the United States. Sanon faces up to life in prison and is scheduled to be sentenced on February 10, 2027.

Prosecutors said South Florida was a planning and financing hub for a scheme to remove Moïse and install a president chosen by the conspirators. They described Sanon as the initial choice and said he helped raise money and arrange travel and lodging. Sanon acknowledged contact with people seeking to replace Moïse but testified that the group had shifted to another candidate before the killing. He denied knowing about a murder plan.

The verdict followed a nearly eight-week trial. Sanon’s lawyer, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defense would appeal. Prosecutors have charged more than 40 people in the case, and a dozen have been convicted, including five serving life terms. Other defendants remain in the U.S. case, and Haiti is scheduled to elect a new president in 2027.

title: How often do you actually regenerate your desiccant?
description: I stopped judging by looks and put a cheap hygrometer in each sealed box. When it drifts above about 30% RH, I recharge loose silica or oven-safe packs at roughly 120 °C for 1.5–2 hours, then cool them in a sealed jar. A 70 °C dryer works too, but it is slow once the beads are heavily loaded. For boxes I open often, that ends up being every 4–8 weeks; long-term storage goes much longer.

title: EU proposes extra €45 billion Ukraine loan, faces fight over guarantees
description:
The European Commission proposed on Nov. 18 an additional €45 billion loan for Ukraine in 2027, covering about two-thirds of a projected €70 billion funding gap. It would supplement the €90 billion EU loan already approved for 2026 and 2027; the new package allocates up to €25 billion for military needs and €20 billion for Ukraine’s state budget. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the funding was intended to strengthen Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Russia. Ukraine would repay the principal only after receiving Russian reparations.

The EU would raise the money on capital markets, with its common budget guaranteeing the borrowing. Budget support would be conditional on Ukrainian reforms, including on the rule of law and corruption. The Commission also wants other international partners to cover the remaining €25 billion of Ukraine’s estimated needs.

Approval faces resistance from Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia, which have signalled they do not want to join the financing. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pressed for all 27 EU members to share responsibility and linked the Ukraine financing to talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget; Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico called that approach “blackmail”. EU leaders are due to discuss the proposal at a Brussels summit on Nov. 26-27, and the budget guarantee requires unanimous member-state backing.

title: Ontario labour board ruling clears path for talks as elementary teachers vote 97% for strike mandate
description:
Ontario’s labour board has ruled that several issues can remain in local bargaining, clearing the way for stalled contract talks to resume as the province’s public elementary teachers and education workers approved strike mandates with 97% support in each vote. The Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario (ETFO), which represents about 84,000 members, said the votes do not mean a strike is imminent and that it remains focused on negotiated agreements.

ETFO said it wants smaller classes, stronger health and safety protections, job security and fair compensation. Bargaining at the union’s two central tables is expected to resume at the end of November. The labour board rejected the government’s effort to move several matters from local to central bargaining, including short-term unpaid leave and transfer, surplus and redundancy timelines, according to ETFO. Education Minister Paul Calandra said the vote results could help bring the parties to the table, while ETFO President David Mastin said they reflected frustration over underfunding and deteriorating school conditions.

title: Waymo suspends US freeway robotaxi rides as California ban persists
description:
Waymo has halted paid driverless freeway rides across the United States after California barred the Alphabet-owned robotaxi company from operating or testing on state freeways following construction-zone and traffic-control incidents. Waymo voluntarily paused freeway service in other markets. Surface-street rides continue, and the company says trained autonomous specialists remain involved in freeway testing.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles says the restriction will remain in force until Waymo demonstrates that it has corrected the identified deficiencies. No public timetable has been given. Waymo says the recent U.S. 101 construction-zone encounters caused no injuries or collisions and that it is working with state officials to resume freeway operations.

The current order follows a similar pause and software recall earlier this year. Waymo resumed freeway rides in late July after changes intended to improve construction-zone detection, but the California agency has again barred driverless freeway operations in the state.

title: IAEA backs US-Saudi nuclear inspections despite safeguards gaps
description:
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi called the inspection arrangements in a planned U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear cooperation agreement “very satisfactory,” although the pact does not include the agency’s Additional Protocol, which enables more intrusive inspections. The U.N. nuclear watchdog approved the separate safeguards text, but the agreement still requires approval by U.S. lawmakers.

The safeguards text grants the IAEA access to sites involved in uranium conversion and enrichment, fuel fabrication and reprocessing, as well as information about those sites. It permits short-notice inspections at declared sites, but does not bar Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium or reprocessing spent fuel—activities that nonproliferation experts identify as potential routes to nuclear weapons. Saudi Arabia has also agreed to additional verification measures on a voluntary basis, Grossi said.

Saudi Arabia has also agreed to additional verification measures on a voluntary basis, Grossi said (al-monitor.com, thehindu.com). Notice periods: Inspectors can receive at least two hours’ notice when already at a covered site; otherwise, the agreement specifies at least 24 hours’ notice (reuters.com, jpost.com). Regional condition: President Donald Trump said in July the agreement depended on Saudi Arabia recognizing Israel; Riyadh has said normalization requires a pathway to Palestinian statehood (timesofisrael.com). Technology exports: U.S. media have reported that the agreement could let Washington export nuclear technology without the usual safeguards designed to prevent future military use (al-monitor.com).

title: German watchdog probes Deutsche Bank after 15 million-file leak
description:
The data-protection commissioner in Germany’s Hesse state opened an investigation into Deutsche Bank on Nov. 18 to examine whether the lender had adequate safeguards for more than 15 million leaked internal records and promptly notified regulators and affected people. Reports based on the files examine past dealings with clients including Russian oligarchs, Jeffrey Epstein and President Donald Trump, and allege that the bank overlooked internal warnings and promoted tax-planning structures for wealthy clients.

The inquiry concerns the handling of the data, not whether the business practices described in the records broke the law. Deutsche Bank said its security testing found no indication that anyone had accessed account information, login credentials or payment data, and that the matters described in the reports dated back years. Its shares fell as much as 6% on Tuesday, Nov. 17; the bank said it did not expect a meaningful financial impact from the disclosures. The regulator has requested further information and documents from the bank.

title: US bank regulator issues AI examiner framework targeting privacy risks
description:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the U.S. regulator for national banks, issued a supervisory framework on Nov. 4 for examiners assessing banks’ use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence. The framework creates no new regulatory requirements but outlines how examiners may assess privacy, cybersecurity, vendor and operational risks.

The framework organizes its considerations into six pillars, including risk, control and oversight. It addresses AI systems that can access sensitive customer information and take actions within bank systems. The article recommends that financial institutions review their AI uses, safeguards and vendor arrangements.

title: Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
description:
Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt.

For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt (cbc.ca, thestar.com). For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027 (cbc.ca, thestar.com). The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing (boereport.com). Meta project: The Sturgeon County complex is a $13-billion, one-gigawatt development expected to come online in two to three years (cbc.ca). Cleanup backlog: The Orphan Well Association lists 7,328 wells awaiting decommissioning and 9,258 sites needing reclamation; it estimates cleanup costs for its inventory at $1.66 billion (cbc.ca, thestar.com). Emissions cap: Bill 42 would eliminate the oil-sands emissions cap, which set a 100-million-tonne limit and had never been enforced; emissions were about 84 million tonnes in 2023 (boereport.com). Public response: A September CBC-commissioned poll found 31% of Albertans strongly opposed data-centre development and another 26% mostly opposed it, with electricity bills and environmental effects among the concerns (cbc.ca).
kite_context:
Perspective: Nathan Ip, Alberta NDP technology critic: Ip said the data-centre provisions do not set clear water-use standards and criticized the rules for exempting already approved projects; he called for a pause on projects while standards are developed (thestar.com, (The Toronto Star)
Perspective: Mark Daley, Western University chief AI officer: Daley said requiring operators to pay for their own power infrastructure is a substantial expense but can also improve electricity generation and transmission for the surrounding community (cbc.ca). (CBC News)
Perspective: Terry Schmidtke, Alberta Small Producers Group chair: Schmidtke said tying cleanup funding to wells through ownership transfers could make smaller producers more confident buying and selling wells while meeting closure obligations (cbc.ca). (CBC News)

title: UK and EU prepare trade reset as Brussels demands Brexit clarity
description:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is due to meet European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on Friday, Nov. 20, as the United Kingdom and European Union seek agreement on food trade, emissions trading, youth mobility and closer security cooperation. A draft would remove many food-trade checks from March 2028, but the emissions agreement has no start date and key terms of the youth scheme remain unsettled.

Brussels wants assurances that UK trade measures will match EU protections, including action on Chinese electric vehicles, before granting Britain access to European industrial support. London is pushing for a weaker commitment. The dispute affects whether British manufacturers can benefit from the EU’s planned “Made in Europe” policies.

The summit is not expected to settle Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc. EU diplomats say they want London to decide what it seeks before opening wider talks. Burnham has said the public will decide the eventual course and Labour’s current election red lines remain in place. He is expected to set out broader options after the summit, with a government plan due in December.

title: Missouri researchers create audit to test AI's reading of interviews
description:
University of Missouri researchers developed a framework to assess whether AI-generated themes capture the meaning of interview responses, not just recurring subjects. They tested it on 32 interviews with nursing faculty, practitioners and students discussing generative AI. For 11 of the 12 themes identified by human researchers, the system generated a similar topic.

Those matches did not guarantee accurate interpretation: the system sometimes merged distinct ideas or split a single theme into smaller topics, and researchers found limited evidence that it consistently uncovered new insights. The study, published in the International Journal of Qualitative Methods, calls for more testing across subject areas and research settings.

title: ‘No one asked for this’: AI is being pushed on people—and they’re sick of it
description:
The AI era is fully here—and while companies bill it as a solution to problems, consequences like mass layoffs, environmental effects, privacy concerns, and the slopification of culture have many people fed up with something they never wanted in the first place.

The technology faces growing resentment from workers, who are being urged to embrace AI tools even as businesses have rushed to reduce their workforces in favor of automation. 

Online, many posts about AI capture a growing frustration with how these tools—and their disruptions—are being forced on users.

“Nobody asked for Google to be worse—but AI made it happen,” one X user recently remarked. “No one asked for computer hardware costs to rise—but AI made it happen. No one asked for human customer service to be replaced—but AI made it happen.”

In another post, Sarah Hoyt, a science fiction, fantasy, and mystery author, said she doesn’t hate artificial intelligence, but is “begging all the crazy people out there to stop pushing AI where no one asked for it.”

The disenchantment plays out in the data: In 2019, 81% of Glassdoor reviews mentioning AI were positive, the company said, compared with 43% this year. Meanwhile, Pew Research found that 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about AI, up from 37% in 2021. And in an Ipsos poll from June, 67% of respondents thought AI would worsen the worker experience.

“The closest analog is the replacement of physical labor throughout the long Industrial Revolution,” said Jiemin Tina Wei, an assistant professor of history at Florida International University. But in this case, it’s “brain work,” rather than manual labor, that’s being replaced. 

“And now, the industries that are getting allegedly wiped out are the ‘low-hanging fruit’ of white-collar work,” she said.

But gutted livelihoods aren’t the only reason many are anti-AI.

The productivity paradox

Louis Hyman, a historian at Johns Hopkins University who specializes in labor and the American economy, points to a “productivity paradox”: a contradiction that was also generally true of the rise of computers in the ’80s, in which similarly dizzying investments didn’t necessarily make people better at their jobs as promised.

He points to snags like the frequency of software updates. “Every time you learn how to do something, suddenly they break it, and you have to relearn it.” With the introduction of AI, it’s “as if all software is being updated, all at once, everywhere.” Another part of the equation, he said, is that it isn’t clear how some people are using AI tools.

Hyman said he uses AI to write software and automate “boring tasks”—for example, he wrote a script to rotate the thousands of photos he takes of historical documents during archive visits so they all face right-side-up. But, he said, “most people are not wanting to sit down and write Python code to automate their job. They just want to do their job.” 

Added to that is the deep fear of being replaced once the work is automated. “I’m a tenured professor—I literally can’t be fired,” he said. “If I automate some boring part of my job, that just means I have more time to do the more interesting parts of my job. And that’s not true for all people, right?” 

A new occupational hazard

Another reason many people push back on AI is the lack of adequate guardrails—especially when it could cause major issues at work.

In one case, an AI tool deleted a software company’s entire database. In another, AI was blamed for deleting a fully edited season of a Swedish reality show mere weeks before the scheduled premiere. In medical settings, AI scribes have put inaccurate information in patient records, raising the question of who would be held liable for resulting medical errors. 

Meanwhile, misreads by AI identification tools used by law enforcement have led to wrongful arrests and injuries, per the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) AI Risk Initiative. Other AI-generated errors have popped up in court documents, federal reports, news stories, and fast-food drive-throughs. 

“The main point I’ve pushed and will continue to push [regarding] AI is ‘no one asked for this,’” radio host Adam Xii said on X, in response to news that Anthropic hallucinated details in its defense during a music copyright lawsuit. “So when a product or service no one asked for suddenly becomes ubiquitous, one must ask: why? Because AI tools are meant to generate more wealth for the wealthy at the expense of creatives.”

At the least, AI’s convenience is being offset by a need to check its work that has created new opportunities for human error. The proliferation of “workslop” even led a tech company’s CEO to fully ban AI use, as Inc. reported this summer. 

“A lot of what I’ve seen is kind of annoyance at the proselytizers at work—or the people who are heavy adopters—creating a lot of extra work for the people around them,” because those people downstream then have to check the work, Wei said.

Wei added that content moderation and data annotation work “can be extremely mentally taxing.” Research has found that “good” challenging work will be both difficult and interesting to certain extents, she said. But checking output is both difficult—because you have to look for every small potential error—and boring.

“You’re not producing knowledge, but merely supervising the production of words, knowledge, content,” Wei said.

The unwanted technological advances continue

AI’s intrusive nature—accompanied, again, by the threat of replacement—is reflected in workers’ behavior, not just in fed-up tweetstorms. One report found that nearly a third of workers surveyed, and 44% among Gen Z, had tried to sabotage their companies’ AI strategies.

Section, an AI planning and upskilling company, recently reported that 69% of workers surveyed said their organization had encouraged the use of AI agents, but only 16% actually used them. And 38% said they use other AI features.

The frustration hasn’t seemed to deter tech companies.

“We heard you wanted Copilot Mode at work,” read an X post from Microsoft that promoted Edge’s Copilot Mode for Business.

“No, you heard wrong,” a computer technician replied. “Literally no one asked for all this AI. In fact, everyone wants to know how to remove it.” 

Questions of organizations

In some cases, it seems companies are starting to discover that automation has some shortcomings.

In the U.S., 32% of hiring managers who eliminated positions in favor of AI have had to reinstate the same or similar roles, according to research from consulting firm Robert Half. Similarly, Gartner predicts that by 2027, half of companies that attributed reductions in staff to AI will rehire people to perform similar work.

Wei said the mismatch between the hopes for AI and the reality of its adoption relates to a quote from Bill Haywood, a famous labor organizer, who said that “the manager’s brains are under the workman’s cap.”

In other words, Wei said, “It’s really ultimately the workers who possess the knowledge and the know-how to run day-to-day operations. Some people have argued that the history of labor is just managers trying to take back that knowledge in an attempt to replace workers in the production.

“And I guess some people experience AI that way—that it’s being [imposed] upon them so that they train, ultimately, their final, automated replacement.”

Hyman said that a better alternative to the “adapt or die” mentality would be for organizations to use the technology to empower their employees. They should “actually say, ‘okay, we’re gonna create organizational conditions that let you replace yourself, and then focus on the work that needs to be done’—because the amount of work to be done is not finite, right?”

“I get told on a nearly weekly basis that historians are going to be replaced,” Hyman said. “So, yeah, it depends on how valuable you think getting reliable information and history is.”

He added that a world “where the only source of history or journalism is from either Open AI or Anthropic” would feel like an “Orwellian nightmare.”

“That seems not a great road to go down,” he said.

title: Bipartisan senators press White House to accelerate AI cyber defenses
description:
U.S. Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds, who belong to opposing parties, urged the White House to coordinate a national response to AI-enabled cyber threats, warning that attackers can find and exploit software flaws faster than many organizations can patch them. Their letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton calls for faster deployment of AI-based defensive tools, security standards for autonomous agents and a meeting among federal agencies, technology developers and critical-infrastructure operators.

The push follows outages affecting banks, technology services and the Federal Aviation Administration. Clayton and other officials said they had found no evidence that the disruptions were part of a coordinated or state-sponsored attack. They attributed the outages to maintenance, upgrades and patching, though the causes of some remained unclear. The senators said patching interconnected systems can take weeks or months and can itself disrupt essential services.

Congressional proposals would also create a federal board to investigate major cyber, AI and technology failures and direct agencies to track and restrict federal AI agents’ access. The senators want the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop standards and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to help deploy defensive tools across banks, hospitals, utilities and government.

title: Officials see AI-driven patching behind outages, not coordinated cyberattack
description:
U.S. intelligence and law-enforcement officials told Congress they found no evidence that the recent service outages were coordinated cyberattacks, while lawmakers and security specialists warned that AI-assisted discovery of software flaws is driving rapid patching on systems not designed for that pace of change. Separately, attackers exploited a flaw in Optimizely’s website experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript onto sites associated with at least 178 organizations. Optimizely said it patched the flaw and removed the code, and officials have not linked that incident to the outages.

Attackers are also using AI tools to locate weaknesses and speed up intrusions. The FBI warned that an AI tool called ARTEX helped hackers gain some privileged access to organizations in less than three hours, while Google reported seeing hackers use AI agents to find vulnerabilities and automate attacks.

The National Security Agency’s classified internal network experienced intermittent service disruptions, prompting staggered staff arrivals while employees used alternative channels. An agency source said classified national-security work continued. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called for a dedicated intelligence red team to examine whether the outages were connected and report to Congress by Dec. 1. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the administration would contact industry about sharing information on major patches before they take effect.

title: ECDC urges hospital infection controls as resistant infections spread in Europe
description:
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said on Nov. 18 that antibiotic-resistant infections continue to spread in Europe, leaving doctors with fewer effective treatment options. More than 70% of the health burden caused by antimicrobial resistance in Europe is linked to healthcare-associated infections, and stronger infection prevention could avert half of that burden, the ECDC said.

The agency called for hand hygiene, protective equipment, prompt detection, isolation of infected patients and effective cleaning in healthcare facilities. It also urged better access to laboratories and adequate infection-control staffing. The ECDC highlighted avoidable antibiotic use for viral illnesses, particularly in children, while Germany’s Robert Koch Institute listed its new ARS-ResistenzCheck data tool among resources for clinical practice.

title: AI-driven flaw discovery strains patching as outages hit US services
description:
AI tools are rapidly uncovering software vulnerabilities and helping automate cyberattacks as outages disrupt U.S. email, flight operations, banking services and an internal National Security Agency communications network. Cybersecurity experts have linked some disruptions to rushed fixes for newly found flaws, but Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the incidents were separate operational problems and officials had no indication of malicious activity or a coordinated attack.

Hackers are also using AI to automate attacks. The FBI said hackers used the Artex AI framework in attacks worldwide, with some gaining privileged access in under three hours, while Palo Alto Networks linked another framework, Cairn, to 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. Researchers also used AI to find Java4Shell, a flaw in Java’s Base64 decoding library that could let an attacker execute commands on a vulnerable server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to patch it.

U.S. regulators sent inquiries to banks affected by outages, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency plans a deeper review of the incidents. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, is separately offering AI-generated fixes to Ubuntu Pro customers through an optional early-release channel before its engineers complete normal review and testing.

excerpt: AI tools are rapidly uncovering software vulnerabilities and helping automate cyberattacks as outages disrupt U.S. email, flight operations, banking services and an internal National Security Agency communications network. Cybersecurity experts have linked some disruptions to rushed fixes for newly found flaws, but Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the incidents were separate operational problems and officials had no indication of malicious activity or a coordinated attack (gizmodo.com, aftenposten.no, rappler.com, fortune.com). Hackers are also using AI to automate attacks. The FBI said hackers used the Artex AI framework in attacks worldwide, with some gaining privileged access in under three hours, while Palo Alto Networks linked another framework, Cairn, to 25 operations against at least 19 organizations (axios.com). Researchers also used AI to find Java4Shell, a flaw in Java’s Base64 decoding library that could let an attacker execute commands on a vulnerable server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to patch it (theconversation.com). U.S. regulators sent inquiries to banks affected by outages, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency plans a deeper review of the incidents (rappler.com). Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, is separately offering AI-generated fixes to Ubuntu Pro customers through an optional early-release channel before its engineers complete normal review and testing (helpnetsecurity.com). Patch volume: Microsoft addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities in November, nearly 20 times the number in the same month a year earlier, Qualys said (rappler.com). Attack scale: CrowdStrike observed one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days last month (axios.com). Vulnerability counts: The industry tracked 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities in 2026, including 1,363 known to have been exploited, VulnCheck said (rappler.com).

title: Vulcan failure linked to fuel supply after loss of Amazon satellites
description:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) said a preliminary review of its Nov. 15 Vulcan rocket failure points to inadequate fuel delivery to its two BE-4 first-stage engines, rather than an engine malfunction. The rocket failed to reach orbit, and all 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites aboard were lost in the first outright mission failure in ULA’s history.

ULA said the first stage underperformed shortly after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow at stage separation for the Centaur V upper stage to complete the mission. The company has not identified which fuel-system component failed or set a return-to-flight date. The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing ULA’s investigation and will review its final report and corrective actions. Amazon’s next Leo launch is scheduled no earlier than Nov. 23 on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

title: US officials say tech outages were separate, not cyberattacks
description:
U.S. intelligence, homeland security and FBI officials told Congress on Nov. 18 that a week of disruptions affecting Microsoft services, air travel, banks, Apple and a National Security Agency communications network resulted from separate technical failures, with no evidence of a coordinated or state-sponsored cyberattack. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed the incidents broadly to maintenance and technical changes, saying systems undergoing patches and upgrades sometimes failed to restart or hand off work as expected.

The failures occurred as companies and agencies rushed to address newly identified software vulnerabilities. Officials and cybersecurity specialists said AI-assisted tools can speed up vulnerability discovery and increase pressure to patch software. But no common cause had been established for the outages: the Federal Aviation Administration disruption involved a router during maintenance, while separate reports attributed failures elsewhere to software or internal updates.

The aviation ground stop lasted more than four hours, and more than 9,100 flights were canceled that Friday. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the department would hold an industry call about notifying customers before planned outages. Banking regulators also contacted lenders, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency planned a deeper review. Microsoft’s next Patch Tuesday is scheduled for Dec. 8.

title: Researchers trace Optimizely malware campaign to three other platforms
description:
Security researchers say malicious code used in the Optimizely breach also appeared on three other website services before reaching 178 organizations through Optimizely’s website-testing service on Nov. 16. Hudson Rock, a cybersecurity firm, found the code on Kissmetrics and StorifyMe on Nov. 13 and on Minute-ly the following Monday. The code appeared on a Philippine bank’s site and a German newspaper’s site through the earlier platforms.

The attackers used Optimizely to inject code aimed at stealing cryptocurrency and payment information. Hudson Rock’s Alon Gal said the forensic evidence points beyond a single-vendor compromise, but how attackers gained access to the other services remains unclear. Optimizely says it detected and blocked the attack, closed the vulnerability within three hours, and that fewer than 5% of its customers were affected. It has hired Mandiant to investigate.

title: Scotland says weakening UK EV rules requires four-nation consent
description:
Scotland’s Transport Secretary Stephen Flynn said any UK move to weaken electric-vehicle sales rules requires the express agreement of all four nations. The UK Climate Change Committee chair, Nigel Topping, has urged Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander to keep the current rules, which require zero-emission vehicles to account for 80% of new car sales by 2030 and all new car sales by 2035. Ministers are considering lowering the 2030 target, with carmakers pressing for a reduction.

The committee says weakening the mandate could leave the UK short of its legally binding climate targets unless ministers find emissions cuts of comparable scale elsewhere. The government says its consultation will not alter its stated phaseout dates for petrol and diesel cars. A decision on the mandate is expected by the end of 2026.

title: EU clears Indonesia trade pact as tariff preferences expire in 2027
description:
European Union governments on Nov. 18 authorized the signing and provisional application of trade and investment agreements with Indonesia, intended to deepen business ties and help offset the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs. The trade deal will remove duties on more than 90% of products and phase out Indonesia’s tariffs of up to 50% on EU cars within five years. The EU estimates annual customs-duty savings of about €600 million.

The parties want to apply the agreements quickly because Indonesia is due to leave the EU’s Generalised Scheme of Preferences on Jan. 1, 2027, ending its preferential tariff treatment under that scheme. The EU and Indonesia must sign the agreements and submit them to the European Parliament for consent; provisional application can begin after both sides complete internal procedures and notify each other.

Farm protections: The deal protects 221 EU geographical indications in Indonesia, while rice, sugar and ethanol are excluded from tariff liberalization and quotas limit access for some other sensitive products (europa.eu). Investment safeguards: The separate investment agreement provides protections against unlawful expropriation and discriminatory treatment, while affirming both sides’ right to regulate for public health, environmental and climate goals (europa.eu). Wider trade: The agreements also cover services, public procurement and intellectual property, and establish cooperation on energy, raw materials and digital trade (europa.eu).

title: EU auditors urge faster PFAS controls as proposed ban nears
description:
The European Court of Auditors warned on Nov. 18 that European Union rules and enforcement are failing to keep pace with per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), persistent chemicals used in consumer goods and industry. Its report says many PFAS remain unregistered, safety limits for food and drinking water rely on outdated evidence, and national checks are inconsistent.

Restricting a substance takes an average of about 11 years, including hazard assessment and the restriction process, auditors said. Bans on individual chemicals can also prompt manufacturers to substitute related compounds with potentially similar risks. A third of EU member states reported no targeted compliance checks between 2020 and 2025.

The auditors urged the European Commission to speed up a bloc-wide restriction, strengthen enforcement and revisit safety limits. The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), the EU chemicals regulator, is expected to deliver its final assessment in December. Draft advice reported by POLITICO proposes temporary exemptions for some uses; the Commission will decide the scope of any restriction.

title: Webb traces Andromeda star merger, challenging common-envelope models
description:
Astronomers say a smaller star spiraled into a red giant and merged with it in the Andromeda galaxy, marking the first closely tracked observation of this stage of binary-star evolution. The system, named AT 2025abao, brightened over several years before erupting in October 2025. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope observed it 47 days after the outburst peaked, helping researchers reconstruct the event.

The team estimates that the giant had seven times the Sun’s mass and the companion about 0.7 times the Sun’s mass. Their interaction ended after about seven orbits, or seven years. The findings, published in Nature on Nov. 18, indicate that energy transport during the shared-envelope phase may be more complex than standard models describe. Researchers say continued observations are needed to determine the remnant’s state and confirm the merger.

excerpt: Astronomers say a smaller star spiraled into a red giant and merged with it in the Andromeda galaxy, marking the first closely tracked observation of this stage of binary-star evolution. The system, named AT 2025abao, brightened over several years before erupting in October 2025. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope observed it 47 days after the outburst peaked, helping researchers reconstruct the event (nasa.gov, sci.news, abc.net.au, sciencenews.org). The team estimates that the giant had seven times the Sun’s mass and the companion about 0.7 times the Sun’s mass. Their interaction ended after about seven orbits, or seven years. The findings, published in Nature on Nov. 18, indicate that energy transport during the shared-envelope phase may be more complex than standard models describe. Researchers say continued observations are needed to determine the remnant’s state and confirm the merger (phys.org, sciencenews.org, newscientist.com, space.com). Ejected material: The eruption expelled an estimated 0.1 to 0.2 solar masses of material, while analysis suggests only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped (sci.news, sciencenews.org). Early evolution: The giant swelled to more than twice its original size while its surface temperature barely changed (sciencenews.org). More candidates: One research team has identified about 30 possible similar mergers, while the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope are expected to search for more (lineadirectaportal.com, abc.net.au).

Perspective: Jason Nordhaus of the Rochester Institute of Technology said nearly one-third of stars may go through the common-envelope phase. That share could be higher if engulfments of planets and other nonstellar objects are included, he said (newscientist.com). (New Scientist)
Quote: "This is probably the most uncertain and critical phase in the evolution of a star" (Jason Nordhaus, New Scientist)

title: Neurologists urge Mediterranean diet as trial links ultraprocessed foods to brain changes
description:
The Spanish Society of Neurology presented guidance on diet and brain health at its annual meeting in Seville, citing evidence for a Mediterranean-style diet and concerns about ultraprocessed foods. The society cited research linking adherence to a Mediterranean diet with at least 12% lower stroke risk and up to 30% lower Alzheimer’s disease risk. It also recommended regular mealtimes, cooking at home and limiting screen use during meals.

Separately, a small Virginia Tech feeding trial found that participants aged 18 to 21 had a reduced response to a milkshake in the brain’s orbitofrontal cortex after two weeks on a diet dominated by ultraprocessed foods. Participants aged 22 to 25 showed no significant change. The study involved 22 people, and researchers said the age-related finding was exploratory. They plan to investigate whether the changes persist and examine effects in younger groups.

title: Israeli lawmakers advance bills to undo Netanyahu-era judicial and media laws
description:
Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, advanced bills on Wednesday to reverse laws affecting the judiciary and broadcast media as the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot seeks to replace caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The move follows the election of Eisenkot ally Matan Kahana as speaker, giving the opposition influence over the chamber’s schedule.

A temporary committee waived the usual 45-day waiting period for the private members’ bills. The measures passed preliminary readings but must still clear further parliamentary stages and three votes before becoming law.

Netanyahu remains in office while Eisenkot negotiates to form a government. Eisenkot’s initial deadline is Dec. 6, with a possible 14-day extension to Dec. 20. If he fails, President Isaac Herzog may give another lawmaker the chance to form a coalition.

title: US communities split over police license-plate cameras and privacy rules
description:
Communities across the United States are taking different approaches to police automated license-plate reader (ALPR) networks: voters in York, Maine, and League City, Texas, rejected their use, while Cedar Rapids approved a nearly $500,000 switch from Flock Safety to Axon without increasing its network of 70 cameras. Springfield, Massachusetts, has not advanced a proposed ban; councilors plan to review possible safeguards before deciding whether to send it forward.

The systems record plates, timestamps and locations. Police say they can help investigate crimes and find missing people, while privacy advocates warn about tracking, misuse and data sharing beyond local jurisdictions. Suffolk County’s sheriff’s office has data-sharing relationships with slightly more than 400 agencies, established through system settings rather than formal written agreements.

Ohio lawmakers are considering House Bill 725, which would set statewide rules for police use of plate data and make misuse a fifth-degree felony. The ACLU of Ohio argues the bill regulates data only after collection and could reduce public access to search information. Springfield’s committee plans to meet again after consulting the city’s Law Department.

title: Pew projects Muslims will surpass Christians globally by 2035
description:
Muslims are projected to become the world’s largest religious group by 2035, reaching 2.57 billion people compared with 2.52 billion Christians, according to new projections from the Pew Research Center. Both populations are expected to grow, but the Muslim population is projected to increase faster, mainly because Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children in 2020-2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women.

Pew estimates there were 2.02 billion Muslims and 2.27 billion Christians in 2020. If current trends continue, the Muslim population will exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, while the Christian population will remain just below 3 billion. The world population is projected to grow 29% over the same period. The report models demographic patterns across 201 countries and territories, including age, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching. Its projections do not account for events such as wars, epidemics or natural disasters.

By 2070, sub-Saharan Africa is expected to be home to more than half of the world’s Christians, while Pakistan is projected to have the largest Muslim population. Pew’s researchers say the projected growth is largely taking place in countries where each faith is already predominant, rather than reflecting a direct shift from one religion to the other.

title: Russian-built Rooppur reactor sends first 370 MW to Bangladesh grid
description:
Bangladesh’s first nuclear power reactor began supplying electricity to the national grid on Nov. 17, when Unit 1 at the Russian-built Rooppur plant was synchronized with the grid at about 40% of its rated power. Its generator produced 370 megawatts at synchronization, said Alexey Likhachev, director general of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom.

The 1,200-MW unit is undergoing a staged startup, with further increases in power and testing required before commercial operation. Rooppur’s two reactors are designed for a combined 2,400 MW; the second unit is expected to follow in 2027.

title: Brazil activates protective measures after about 20 isolated Awá approach
description:
About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks.

Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

title: North Carolina utility commissioner resigns after Duke rate decisions
description:
North Carolina utilities commissioner Donald van der Vaart will resign Jan. 1, 2027, days after the state approved Duke Energy rate increases and new requirements for large data centers. The decisions raise electricity charges for Duke customers over two years, with the first increases taking effect in January 2027.

State Treasurer Brad Briner said Wednesday he accepted van der Vaart’s resignation, effective four and a half years before his term was due to end. The announcement gave no reason for his departure. Van der Vaart missed the Duke Energy Carolinas vote, dissented in part in the Duke Energy Progress decision and did not participate in a separate decision on a long-term energy plan. Briner said he expects to name a replacement in the coming days or weeks. Consumer advocates are urging Attorney General Jeff Jackson to appeal the rate order. His office says it is reviewing the decision, and he has 30 days to appeal.

title: COP31 ministers face deadlock over fossil fuels, finance and science
description:
Ministers at the United Nations COP31 climate summit in Antalya remained deadlocked Wednesday over a final agreement, with 21 issues unresolved and only days left before the conference’s scheduled close Friday, Nov. 20. Disputes include whether to call for a transition away from fossil fuels, how to fund climate adaptation and whether to set a global electrification goal.

A draft political deal released Monday included competing proposals on fossil fuels, climate finance, the 1.5°C goal, science and trade. Turkey’s proposal to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use to 35% by 2035 has support from 75 countries, but some governments oppose including it in the final text.

Countries also disagree over when the next assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed climate science body, should be ready. Vulnerable countries want them before the 2028 global review, while others favor 2029. Ministers met informally Wednesday to seek compromises; a revised draft was expected Thursday.

Disputes include whether to call for a transition away from fossil fuels, how to fund climate adaptation and whether to set a global electrification goal (un.org, theguardian.com, biobiochile.cl). A draft political deal released Monday included competing proposals on fossil fuels, climate finance, the 1.5°C goal, science and trade. Turkey’s proposal to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use to 35% by 2035 has support from 75 countries, but some governments oppose including it in the final text (dawn.com, rfi.fr, un.org). Countries also disagree over when the next assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed climate science body, should be ready. Vulnerable countries want them before the 2028 global review, while others favor 2029. Ministers met informally Wednesday to seek compromises; a revised draft was expected Thursday (nagariknetwork.com, un.org, biobiochile.cl). Unequal access: More than 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity in 2024; electricity accounts for about 12% of Africa’s energy use, compared with roughly a quarter in Europe (rfi.fr). Science funding: The IPCC has not set its budget for next year, potentially delaying a scientific report needed ahead of next year’s UN climate conference (insideclimatenews.org). Ocean commitments: More than 95% of coastal and island nations include ocean measures in their climate plans, but about 60% of those commitments depend on additional finance or technical support (europeansting.com). title: Italy makes IHRA antisemitism definition law, prompting free-speech dispute
description:
Italy’s parliament gave final approval on Nov. 17 to a law incorporating the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism into the country’s legal framework, with 147 votes in favour, 93 against and five abstentions. The Senate had approved the measure in March. Debate focused on whether the definition’s examples involving Israel could blur the line between antisemitism and political criticism.

The law sets policy guidelines rather than creating new offences or penalties. It establishes a national coordinator and a three-year strategy covering incident monitoring, online hate, education and the security of Jewish communities. Italy already had laws against incitement and hate crimes; the new measure gives public authorities a statutory reference for identifying antisemitism.

The government says criticism of Israeli policy remains protected, while Amnesty International and opposition lawmakers warn that the definition could encourage censorship or self-censorship, including in schools and universities. Supporters point to 963 antisemitic incidents recorded in Italy in 2025, nearly four times the 2022 figure. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s governing coalition and centrist parties backed the measure; the Democratic Party, Five Star Movement and Green-Left Alliance opposed it.

title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
description: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.

title: Gulf states condemn Iranian strikes as Kuwait reserves right to respond
description:
Kuwait said it reserves the right to take all necessary measures to defend its territory after Iranian drones targeted U.S.-linked assets at Ali Al Salem air base. Iran said it targeted Patriot systems and launch platforms, while Kuwait reported interceptions. The attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain were part of renewed Iran-U.S. exchanges after a U.S. strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Nov. 17.

Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted several attacks, and authorities issued two shelter alerts before giving an all-clear. Kuwait did not report damage or casualties in its account of the interceptions.

Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said one crew member was missing and 11 were injured after an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The other crew members were evacuated. Qatar condemned the strikes and called for dialogue and diplomatic solutions.

title: Age-Related Synaptic Dysfunction and Possible Approaches to Treatment
description: Dysfunction of the synaptic connections between neurons in the brain is characteristic of aging and exaggerated in neurodegenerative conditions, particularly Alzheimer's disease. The brain is a collection of neural networks: a neuron extends branching axons that connect to other neurons via synapse structures. When synapses lose function, the network loses function, and cognitive decline is the result. Here, researchers discuss the biochemistry of synapses and a variety of approaches to therapy that might improve matters. They conclude that the most promising approaches at the present time are those focused on reducing the impact of aging on the function of glial cells. title: ECB warns AI debt boom could spread losses across markets
description:
The European Central Bank warned on Nov. 18 that debt-funded investment in artificial intelligence, stretched valuations and strained government finances could threaten euro-area financial stability. Big technology companies had more than $4 trillion in off-balance-sheet commitments by the second quarter of 2026. Those obligations, tied in part to data centers and advanced chips, function economically like debt, the ECB said.

The bank said a shift in investor sentiment could spread losses from technology shares to bond markets, while geopolitical uncertainty and higher energy costs could add pressure. It judged euro-area banks able to absorb shocks but identified greater vulnerabilities at some non-bank financial firms, where safeguards are less developed. Separately, Anthropic, the maker of Claude AI models, was expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19 after setting the price of its initial public offering the previous day.

Repayment risks: Higher energy prices and weaker economic conditions could make it harder for households and firms to repay debts. title: Chad study finds eagles may prey on 26-kilogram baboons
description:
Researchers have found marks on bones and skulls suggesting Verreaux’s eagles preyed on adult male olive baboons in Chad’s Ennedi Plateau, including one estimated to have weighed 26.2 kilograms. The study, published Nov. 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, challenges a longstanding rule of thumb that primates above about 13 kilograms were effectively beyond avian predation. Previously, no primate heavier than that had been confirmed killed by a raptor.

The team documented punctured eye sockets and talon-like scrapes on shoulder blades among the baboon remains. It did not witness a kill, so the researchers describe eagle predation as a likely explanation rather than a directly observed event. Some early hominins were in a similar weight range, but the findings do not establish that eagles hunted adult hominins or influenced their defensive behavior. The researchers plan further study of the isolated baboon population and its behavior.

Sample details: The initial sample contained nine baboons, including eight adult males; researchers estimated a mean body mass of 22.2 kilograms (wiley.com, gizmodo.com). Bone evidence: Two males had punctured eye sockets, and researchers identified a scapula with scrapes in a pattern associated with eagle feeding (wiley.com, discovermagazine.com). Possible defense: Researchers observed baboons sounding alarm calls and moving to safety when Verreaux’s eagles flew overhead; primates may also mob aerial predators by charging them (discovermagazine.com, gizmodo.com).

title: EU agrees to streamline permits for renewable projects and power grids
description:
The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on Nov. 18 to speed up permitting for renewable energy projects, electricity grids and storage facilities, aiming to reduce construction delays and strengthen energy security. The changes also cover recharging stations and authorizations for new electricity and gas infrastructure.

The agreement streamlines deadlines for approvals and grid connections and provides for digital portals to handle applications. Both institutions must still endorse and formally adopt it after a legal and linguistic review; member states will then have 18 months to incorporate the directive into national law.

title: European disease agency warns resistant bacteria threaten hospital treatment
description:
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warned on Nov. 18 that antibiotic-resistant bacteria continue to spread across Europe, leaving doctors with fewer effective treatments. Its European Antibiotic Awareness Day alert called for urgent, sustained action. More than 35,000 people die each year from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in the European Union and European Economic Area. More than 70% of Europe’s AMR health burden is linked to multidrug-resistant infections acquired in healthcare settings.

The ECDC said resistant infections could make it harder or impossible to safely carry out organ transplants, cancer chemotherapy and intensive care. It called for coordinated infection prevention, careful antibiotic prescribing, stronger laboratory capacity and surveillance. Faster genomic monitoring can help track the spread of resistant strains and guide treatment decisions, it said.

title: Malaysia pardons board minutes expose split over Najib house arrest
description:
Minutes from Malaysia’s Sept. 18 Federal Territories Pardons Board meeting show Attorney-General Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar and Federal Territories Minister Hannah Yeoh opposed allowing former Prime Minister Najib Razak to serve his remaining prison term at home. They argued that house arrest had no basis in statute. King Sultan Ibrahim nevertheless approved the conditional arrangement, which took effect after a court order on Nov. 10.

Former lawmaker Tony Pua shared the minutes online. The records were reportedly declassified for a court challenge, but politicians are demanding confirmation of their authenticity and clarification of who authorized their release. Higher Education Minister Zambry Abdul Kadir said the Cabinet had not discussed declassification; Barisan Nasional (BN) MPs sought an official clarification within 24 hours. The Malaysian Bar Council’s legal challenge argues that the constitution does not authorize house detention and asks the courts to consider the arrangement’s legal basis.

title: Trump and Marcos announce trade deal before planned Xi-Putin talks
description:
President Donald Trump and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced a trade deal in Manila on Wednesday, ahead of Trump’s planned talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday. Trump called it a major agreement, but the leaders did not publicly detail its terms. The announcement followed Trump’s Manila meetings with Southeast Asian leaders and the first summit in two years of the Quad, which comprises the United States, Japan, India and Australia.

The Quad’s joint statement expressed concern over economic coercion and arbitrary export restrictions without naming a country. Leaders also outlined maritime patrol exercises for 2027 and continued cooperation on an artificial-intelligence accelerator. Trump said the Quad would invest more than $85 million to expand access to trusted AI ecosystems across the Indo-Pacific.

Trump’s brief visit to the Philippines also drew protests over his policies and Pax Silica, a U.S.-led supply-chain initiative. Human Rights Watch said police detained at least 245 protesters, including farmers, journalists and children. Trump is due to travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and the scheduled three-leader meeting on Nov. 19.

title: Moment Energy launches certified second-life battery system for businesses
description:
Canadian battery repurposer Moment Energy has launched Nova, a commercial and industrial storage system built with retired electric-vehicle batteries and rated at 200 kilowatts and 500 kilowatt-hours. It has UL safety certifications and independent verification under U.S. foreign-entity sourcing rules, which the company says could qualify it for federal investment tax credits from 2027.

Orders opened Nov. 18, 2026, with first deliveries expected in the first quarter of 2027. Nova can discharge at full power for two hours; Moment says its compact design is intended for sites including hospitals, airports and manufacturing facilities.

title: Amazon and Google to own 28% of AI firm Anthropic
description:
Amazon and Google are set to own a combined 28.4% of Anthropic after the Claude developer’s public offering and a separate private placement, making two of its largest cloud customers major shareholders. Anthropic’s filing describes Amazon, Google and Microsoft as investors, customers, distribution partners and competitors.

Customers can access Claude through their existing cloud accounts, while providers handle billing and retain a fee before passing the remainder to Anthropic. Technology analysts say public-company reporting may give enterprise buyers more visibility into Anthropic’s operations, while quarterly pressure to show growth could prompt it to seek longer contracts and firmer spending commitments.

Anthropic is scheduled to begin trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19, becoming the first pure-play frontier AI lab on public markets, according to Morningstar. Its filings and quarterly disclosures will detail its AI business and ties to cloud infrastructure providers.

title: US officials say no evidence links outages to cyberattacks as disruptions hit NSA, Apple
description:
U.S. officials said they have found no evidence that coordinated cyberattacks caused a series of technology failures affecting banks, airlines, major software services and government networks, after disruptions reached the National Security Agency (NSA) and Apple on Tuesday, Nov. 17. The incidents followed a Microsoft service outage, a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop and disruptions at JPMorgan Chase and United Airlines. Agencies and companies have cited separate technical causes.

excerpt: Fill shoe boxes with toys, cloths and craft supplies to children overseas this Christmas through Evangelical Free Church for this year’s Operation Christmas Child drive. The deadline's Nov. 22. Williams Lake residents have until Sunday, Nov. 22 to drop off gift-filled shoeboxes at Evangelical Free Church for this year’s Operation Christmas Child drive. Operation Christmas Child is a Samaritan’s Purse project that works with local churches and ministries overseas to distribute gift-filled shoeboxes to children at Christian outreach events. Shetler suggested packing school supplies, hygiene items, a toy or craft kit and something to wear, such as a hat or gloves. Donors can choose to pack for a child ages two to four, five to nine or 10 to 14. Shetler asked donors to leave out candy, liquids, toothpaste, soap, glass items and war-themed toys. Shetler thanked Williams Lake residents for their generosity over the years. “It’s such an expression of love and compassion to children around the world that do not have much,” she said. Empty shoeboxes and brochures are available at the Evangelical Free Church, 1100 North 11th Ave., and at Kit and Kaboodle, 83A Second Ave. S. Filled shoeboxes can be dropped off at the church through Sunday, Nov. 22. Shetler said the boxes will travel through Kamloops to Calgary, where they’ll be checked before being shipped overseas.

title: Small study links appetite-suppressing drugs to low nutrient intake
description:
A small exploratory study found that some people taking appetite-suppressing medicines such as Wegovy and Mounjaro consumed too little energy and key nutrients and had limited awareness of the potential shortfalls. Researchers asked 14 patients at one English general practice—10 treated privately and four through the National Health Service—to recall what they ate over two days. Average intake was 1,231 calories a day, or 58.5% of estimated energy needs; three participants reported less than 800 calories daily.

Participants linked their reduced intake to appetite suppression and described a lack of structured follow-up and dietary advice. Researchers cautioned that the observational study, based on a small group from one relatively affluent practice, cannot establish cause and effect and may not apply widely.

title: COP31 draft proposes $120 billion in annual adaptation finance by 2035
description:
A draft COP31 agreement proposes at least $120 billion a year in adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035, alongside accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels. Released by the conference presidency on Nov. 16, the text remains under negotiation and does not represent an agreed position; the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, are scheduled to end Nov. 20.

African negotiators are pressing for predictable grants, measurable delivery milestones and finance that does not deepen debt. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024. Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for funding to restore land and rivers damaged by mining and for greater local processing of Africa’s minerals.

Released by the conference presidency on Nov. 16, the text remains under negotiation and does not represent an agreed position; the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, are scheduled to end Nov. 20 (frontpageafricaonline.com, premiumtimesng.com, sciencesetavenir.fr). African negotiators are pressing for predictable grants, measurable delivery milestones and finance that does not deepen debt. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024. Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for funding to restore land and rivers damaged by mining and for greater local processing of Africa’s minerals (allafrica.com, myjoyonline.com). Access procedures: The draft would simplify funding approvals and ask climate funds to publish how long applicants wait for approval and their first payment (allafrica.com). Loss and damage: The draft cites about $2.8 billion in requests under the fund’s Barbados Implementation Modality against roughly $342 million available, and says only half of the $822 million pledged had been paid in (premiumtimesng.com). Energy divide: The proposed text also calls for electricity to account for 35% of final energy use by 2035, but African negotiators say it must prioritize access and recognize countries’ different starting points (premiumtimesng.com, frontpageafricaonline.com). Liberia’s shortfall: Liberia says about $360 million in climate-finance commitments under its previous climate plan remained undisbursed as of December 2024; 54 percentage points of its 2035 emissions-reduction target depend on international support (frontpageafricaonline.com).
